Brushes included: Pinnacle foundation brush, angled concealer brush

What Are the Best Makeup Brushes Worth Shopping?

According to Erickson, the most essential makeup brushes in your set are the ones you use with powder products, such as bronzer, blush, or setting powder. "Everyone should own a small powder brush—or even something that resembles a large eyeshadow brush—to cut shine where needed and set concealer. An angled brush can be helpful when using bronzer or contour, as well as a medium-sized cheek brush for powder blush."

And when it comes to eye makeup brushes, the expert adds, "It can be helpful to have a dual-sided angled brush-spoolie combo for brows, as well as for winged liner. A small, dense, pointed brush for the lash line and inner corner is nice to have, as well as one or two blending brushes for the eyelids."

Should I Opt for Synthetic or Natural Bristles?

"I like to say there is nothing 'natural' about animal hair," Anisa Telwar Kaicker tells Bazaar. "It can dry faster and break more quickly. Man-made synthetics can be long-lasting, hygienic, innovative in shape, and soft to the touch."

Erickson agrees that synthetic makeup brushes outperform products made using animal by-products. "Synthetic brushes tend to be more durable and last longer. Less and less natural bristles areused today, and as a makeup artist, I don’t think we need them, performance-wise."

What’s the Most Effective Way to Clean Makeup Brushes?

"When I deep clean my makeup brushes once or twice a month, I typically use Dr. Bronner’s 18-in-1 castile soap," Erickson notes. "At the very least, use a quick-dry brush cleaner like Sephora’s Daily Brush Cleaner between each use to avoid the spread of bacteria."

Telwar Kaicker suggests that after deep cleaning, you remove excess water from your brushes with a towel. Then, tilt the brush downward to prevent water from seeping into the ferrule and breaking down the glue in the brush head.

How Often Should I Replace My Makeup Brushes?

According to Erickson, high-quality, well-cared-for brushes can last for years. "If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. I’ve had some of my makeup brushes last a decade and some only last a year or two. If you love it and you’re able to properly sanitize it, use it for as long as you can."

How do you know when it's time for a new set? Erickson says it all comes down to the glue. "Typically, when a makeup brush goes bad, the glue between the brush and handle starts to break down due to wear and moisture from cleaning. When that happens, toss it and move on. For beauty blenders and sponges that harbor bacteria, toss them after a few uses, no matter how well you sanitize them. Toss after a few uses, especially if you’re acne-prone."

#6621. The Woven Tote Bag Trend Is Taking Over Runways and Workdays

Woven bags have officially reached icon status.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Is there any other bag that works as hard in real life as the tote bag? When it comes to being on duty and looking good, probably not. The humble tote has come in all iterations: lightweight cotton, supple leather, and suede. But more recently, the runways have been obsessed with making the oversize tote-style bags in luscious jumbo woven iterations. We saw them on the spring/summer 2027 runways at Dries Van Noten, Courrèges, Bottega Veneta, and Altuzarra. And then, labels like Bembien, Naghedi, and Dragon Diffusion are pumping out woven totes like there’s no tomorrow.

A big woven bag offers up texture and interest in a sea of ubiquitous canvas logo totes. It also gives you a bit of resilience so you don’t have to baby your bag on, say, a subway commute or a brisk morning walk where the risk of bumping into others is second nature. It is the working girl’s best friend. That’s just one of the reasons why fashion retailers have fallen head over heels for the style lately.

“Regardless of lifestyle, everyone needs a bag that carries a lot, and potentially the kitchen sink,” Ryan Kleman, Moda Operandi’s VP of buying, accessories, tells ELLE. The great news about a woven bag is that it also seamlessly goes with everything. Tone it down for a day at the office with a button-down top or a casual dress, or take it out for a nice dinner; a silk scarf tied about the strap can be the pop of color or embellishment you might crave for a more formal occasion.

In the case of some of these brands, the woven tote is literal fashion history. Bottega Veneta, for example, first introduced its signature “Intrecciato” woven leather technique in 1975. The fashion house’s spring/summer 2027 collection modernized the technique by applying it to enormous, hulking bags that swayed when worn over the shoulder. Paired with layered sweaters and matching leather belts, the bags felt like a decidedly fresh take on wearable artisanship by creative director Louise Trotter.

In the case of Dries Van Noten, one model carried an absolutely huge woven raffia-effect foldover clutch. Styled with a heather gray hoodie rolled up to reveal leather bubblegum-pink opera gloves with a biker-style cutout and buckle at the hand, the bag itself proved just how versatile a woven piece can be.

If you’re indeed thinking of upgrading your everyday work bag for a woven tote, it’s better to think bigger. “The oversized scale of the bags and the woven construction provide the perfect details to convert a chore into a fashion statement,” says Kleman. “At Moda, we have dubbed this trend the Big A** Bag and our customers are loving it.” This, too, is true: the bigger the weave, the better the carryall.

#6620. 26 Best Men's Scarves 2026, According to GQ Editors

Are any accessories as essential, yet mysteriously overlooked, as the best men's scarves? First, they warm your neck (and face, and chest) like nothing else. Second, they put a style-forward, cheery, colorful bow on pretty much any outfit. And yet, these soft little miracles are all too often an afterthought in the menswear world. Even if you’re the type of guy to painstakingly lay your fits out the night before, chances are when it comes to your scarf game, you’re still reaching for one you picked up in a rushed pinch from Nordstrom Rack, or at a frigid college football game.

This is, of course, fine. But it’s also sort of a tragedy. Because when you pick up a truly great scarf, everything changes. Swaddling your neck in cashmere (or cashmere-emulating fabrics) doesn’t just provide a soothing all-day embrace through bracing winds. It also, like a necktie, creates an opportunity for a flash of personal style, right under your handsome face. Even better, because scarves use less fabric than coats and knitwear, they’re also a great way to own some of the best materials in our industry for far less scratch.

To help you pick the one you’ll soon be recognized by, I surveyed hundreds of scarves from across the fashion (and budget) spectrum, journeying from mall chains, to historic British manufacturers, to the buzziest makers today, and everything in-between. Below, the final 26 best men's scarves to knot up this winter—and next winter, and the one after that.

Parisian label Brut puts a Big Apple spin on the classic European football supporter scarf, featuring none other than Lady Liberty herself. A fitting French connection.

The bandana, neckerchief, foulard, whatever you want to call it has become an easy, even trendy winter accessory. Alex Mill’s is made from extra-fine merino wool, comes in 14 colors, and costs less than a hundo.

Another bandana-shaped style from the Banana, this time with a generous helping of cashmere for a little extra softness.

A smart tartan plaid as classic as the linings inside Barbour’s famous wax jackets, in a soft wool-cashmere blend. About as British as a rainy afternoon and a pint at the pub.

We cross the Irish Sea for L.L.Bean’s take, made from Irish-woven lambswool, known for its durability and natural water resistance. Plenty warm and handsome to boot.

Lost & Found’s Scottish lambswool scarf comes with pockets stitched into it. Perfect for stashing your cards, cash or other things a little less above board. We won’t ask.

Another triangle scarf, here in a stunning sienna color that’s still right in Margaret Howell’s wheelhouse. Snug and sensible.

Lil’ brown checks, a fuzzy brushed finish, and Japanese cotton-wool twill woven in England. A big helping of understated charm.

A nice change of pace from the usual winter plaids, two-tone chevrons give this Coach scarf a little graphic punch, while a lightweight but warm alpaca blend keeps things cosy.

If you love pattern, fall and winter is primed for Polo Power. This Fair-Isle-esque design is easier to wear than the classic sweater, and will add some energy to your winter fits.

All the cozy, old-school charm of an Aran knit, Percival takes the classic cream cable-knit sweater and turns it into a scarf. And at more than half off, it’s a bit of a steal.

She's pricey, but you’re paying for fine Scottish-spun cashmere materials and serious know-how with an entirely handmade and hand-linked scarf.

Printed scarves were the first things Drake’s made back in 1977, when it was still a small workshop. These archival designs are works of art you can wear. Wool, silk and good taste.

Missoni’s famous zigzags came out of swinging ’60s Milan, and they still have that groovy Italian charm. Funny how something so unmistakably of its time never seems to go out of style.

A statement scarf if there ever was one, with vibrant Yves Klein blue and an oversized logo patch that’s not shy about announcing itself. A lot to spend on yourself, maybe, but one hell of a gift.

NN07 mixes two old-school patterns into one elegant Italian-woven scarf, with a fuzzy brushed finish and blanket-stitched edges. Your granddad would approve.

This fashion-guy-approved cashmere scarf from Auralee is classic enough, but boy, those rich colours are doing something for me. It truly is all in the details.

By now, you may have noticed the Scots know a thing or two about wool. Johnstons of Elgin has been at it for centuries, and this beautifully woven cashmere scarf is further proof.

#6618. Design Experts Reveal When It’s Actually OK to Start Decorating for the Holidays

There’s no hard rule—but your HOA may have one.

Now that the Halloween candy bowls are empty, you might find thoughts of tinsel, garland, and fairy lights dancing in your head, but is it really time to trade your pumpkins for holiday trimmings? Some have strong opinions on the topic, half believing the jolly spirit of the holiday season doesn't start until after Thanksgiving, the other rushing to unbox their silver bells as soon as the clock strikes 12 on November 1—but the choice isn’t always yours to make.

If you belong to a Homeowners’ Association (and over 78.1 million Americans do), the question of when to put up your outdoor décor may be dictated by their guidelines. HOAs tend to have rules about holiday decorations, restrictions covering their location (within the boundaries of your yard, of course), sound level (not too loud), safety (no open flames), light color, and when the decorations can be installed. In some communities, you can even be fined for bringing out the twinkle lights and nativity creche before Thanksgiving—this happened to one Florida man in 2002, when he was hit with a fine of $1,000 for putting his lights up on November 6.

If you don’t live in an HOA, you may not get fined for decorating too early, but you will get judged by neighbors who find pre-Thanksgiving holiday displays a little, well, tacky. To be fair, holding until after Thanksgiving does have its perks—why would you pass on the opportunity to decorate a gorgeous fall tablescape? In the spirit of peace on earth and goodwill toward man, we asked design experts what to do. Here’s what they said.

Additional copy by Meghan Shouse and Alyssa Khan.

You might follow a religious tradition that guides your holiday decorating, like placing the Baby Jesus in the nativity on Christmas Day or keeping the tree up until Epiphany. But when it comes to secular etiquette, there are no hard-and-fast rules about when to start (or stop) decking the halls.

“Most people find it tasteful to stick within the weeks or the month of the holiday itself,” points out Lizzie Post, co-president of The Emily Post Institute and author of Emily Post’s Etiquette—The Centennial Edition. “That said, there is no etiquette that dictates it. It’s the same way you can paint your house neon orange with blue stripes—there’s nothing that says you can’t. It’s really, do you want to be the person who does?”

For designer Tan France, the answer to that question is decidedly yes. For the past decade, he and his husband have been decorating their tree on Halloween and taking it down on Valentine’s Day. “I’m British, and we don’t really do Halloween,” he explains. “When I moved here 16 years ago, I was more obsessed with Christmas. So on Halloween day, when everyone else is crafting their costumes, I want to be decorating the tree. And a tree brings my husband and me a lot of joy when we come down and turn the lights on first thing in the morning. It’s just a lovely thing to perk your day up.”

Do people question France about his decision to put up decorations so early, and for so long? “Oh gosh, yeah, everyone asks that,” he says. “Online, the press, neighbors. And my answer is really simple: Why delay joy?”

If you are jonesing to do some holiday decorating, there's good news: While Christmas might be weeks away, there is one happening right now. It’s called Thanksgiving.

“Anytime before midnight of Thanksgiving is too early to decorate,” insists Wendy Kerrigan, founder of Atelier Design in New Orleans. “Filling the house with Christmas decorations too soon really takes away from the beauty of Thanksgiving, moving your mind into the bustle of Christmas.”

Kerrigan wishes more people would celebrate the fall season for longer; rushing to the tinsel takes away from the beauty of the autumn season, “Thanksgiving can be experienced in a special way too, filling the house with fall colors, fall leaves, gourds, and cornucopia,” says Kerrigan. “Instead of trying to hurry the year along, enjoy each family celebration for what it is.”

Even more, sprinting to the Yuletide season robs the holiday of its own magic. “What makes things special when they’re once a year is that they’re experiences you look forward to,” says Vermont-based interior designer Joshua Smith. “How many holidays can we take at one time? Are we doing Black Friday in July now? Let’s just enjoy the season that we’re in!”

When it comes to holiday decorating, many hands make light work. Several designers say they take advantage of the long holiday weekend and enforced family time to rope in some extra help making spirits bright. “In my parents' home, we start decorating right after Thanksgiving dinner. It’s a rare opportunity for everyone to be together, and my siblings and I stay to help out our parents,” says New York-based designer Mikel Welch. “Plus, it’s a much better tradition than terrorizing sales associates on Black Friday Eve!"

Smith has a plan for bringing the Christmas spirit to his home, without shouldering the burden of doing all the hall-decking himself. Last year, his family decorated their trees over Thanksgiving weekend and made it a tree-decorating contest. With his husband's family in town, “they’ll be divided into three teams, decorating three trees, and I’ll go around at the end judging, and everyone will win prizes. We’re not all going to be together at Christmas, so this activity is a fun way to celebrate the season and not do all the work myself,” he says.

Still, early decorators would argue that the amount of effort needed to set up holiday decor is another reason to put up decorations early—and keep them up late. “This is the most miserable time of the year; it gets dark so early, it’s so darn cold. I just think you should do everything you can to bring yourself joy,” says France. “Why put in all that effort for a few weeks?”

Even those who are normally on the side of waiting to decorate agree that desperate times call for dopamine decorating. Whether it’s the state of your inbox or the state of the world that is stressing you out, if you’re feeling a little blue, go right ahead and pull out the red and green.

“In a perfect calendar, the day after Thanksgiving would be my official start to the holiday season—it's traditionally the day when my family goes out into the woods of Tahoe National Forest to chop down our tree, drag it home, and decorate it,” says designer Noz Nozawa of Noz Design. “But this year, the day after Halloween is when I let the holidays start—there's plenty to worry about, and having my nutcrackers and string lights out a few weeks early can only boost spirits.”

Whenever you decorate, it can be a way to bring fun to a not-always joyful world. “We have no control over a lot of things in our lives, but when we walk through the door of our home, we choose to focus our energy and attention on whether that is on fear or on love and joy,” says Smith. “And this holiday season, I think more than ever we have to focus on ways to bring more light to ourselves and to each other.”

When it comes to early decor, “I can handle it from my neighbor; I cannot handle it from a corporation,” says Post. That may be because we know the Christmas displays popping up in a big-box store alongside the Halloween candy are trying to sell us something, while a neighbor decorating is spreading joy, spending their own time and money to brighten the dark winter nights. For a shop, holiday decorating is mercenary. For an individual, it’s a mitzvah.

If you appreciate the joy inspired by holiday displays and do want to start setting them up early or keep them up late, consider finding a middle ground by leaning toward decor that’s more about lighting up the night, rather than marking a particular occasion. “I see a lot of people in Vermont leaving the actual lights up, not so much like blow-up Santas or things like that, but the actual lights up for the entire winter,” says Post.

If you’re a minimalist (or live in a studio apartment), you don’t need a tree to decorate. “If you don’t have a tree, I’m going to invite you to place a hurricane lamp on your coffee table with a wreath of greenery around it and light a candle in the evening,” says Smith. “Because what we know from neuroscience and neuroaesthetics is, you’ve got to engage the senses to nourish the soul!” Light a candle or turn on some twinkle lights, and you’re liable to spark joy as well.

France would argue that even his trees aren’t occasion-specific. “Here’s the thing: I’m Muslim, and my tree and the lights on our house aren’t necessarily for Christmas,” he explains. “It’s to celebrate Thanksgiving, Christmas, and the New Year. This is the most miserable time of the year. It gets dark so early, it gets light so late, it’s so darn cold. I just think do everything you can to bring yourself joy.”

Though you’d never find them rushing to hang their stockings, the designer duo behind the Kansas City-based firm Kobel + Co, Elizabeth Bennett and Mallory Robins, say there’s one design scheme you can always tap into if you find yourself in the class of outliers running to get decor up before Christmas Eve. “Ralph Lauren Holiday isn't just having a moment; it's a classic holiday go-to for so many reasons,” Bennett explains. “Warm crimsons, rich browns, tactile fabrics, and blue-green plaids make a beautiful holiday palette. Layer in antique silver pieces and simple glass ornaments. A little patina and variation keep everything from feeling too matched. The goal is a warm, welcoming home with pieces that feel collected and personal.” After all, you want it to feel like home, even at Christmas.

#6616. Misha & Puff’s First Womenswear Collection Gives Knitwear a New Point of View

The cult-favorite children’s knitwear brand is officially expanding to adults.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Women’s fashion has some of the best designs out there—full stop. That said, every now and then I see a well-dressed kid and think, “Damn, I wish I had something like that.” This is especially true when I see a little one sporting a design from none other than Misha & Puff, a brand known for its ethically crafted, handmade, vintage-inspired children’s clothes. And while my wardrobe carries a playful touch, I’m not necessarily looking for a supersized version of a child’s sweater, but rather the essence of that whimsy. Thankfully, I don’t have to look too far; Misha & Puff just launched its first-ever women’s collection—and it’s more than I could have hoped for.

“Knits are hot. Knits are sexy. The way that they drape, the way that they accentuate your neck, I really do feel like we can do a lot with a knit,” Sophia Roe told ELLE.com over the phone. “For me, I feel really beautiful when I put these clothes on.” The James Beard Award-winning chef—along with her daughter, Mizu—came together with artist Mara Hoffman behind the lens to create a campaign that captures the essence of Misha & Puff, highlighting the craftsmanship and expression of the brand’s new womenswear collection.

“Everything I do with the brand is very authentic and really about what I’m interested in...That’s how the kids’ brand started, with me having my son and then growing up,” Misha & Puff’s founder, Anna Wallack, said on a phone call. “The choice to launch women’s in a bigger way really comes from the pull that I’m feeling as a woman. For me, dressing women and dressing myself is about how we’re working these pieces together. How do I feel in these silhouettes? Who is this character today? I want to keep playing with that in a bigger way.”

Wallack went on to tell me that designing for the collection—which launched today—started with what she described as a “fiber-first” approach. “We work with a Pima cotton in Peru that worked so well for kids because it’s incredibly soft and it’s so wearable, and then to find that I want to wear that all the time for myself; I want to wear our merino wool,” she explained. “Our decision to launch women’s with a bigger collection really was a commitment to doing it instead of just making one sweater here and there.” The result? A range of expressive knits in a color palette reminiscent of the ’70s that encourage the wearer to be who she is as a woman today. With every solid- or heather-hued piece there’s another featuring an eye-catching print or embroidery detail. “I feel a little more permission to explore other ideas in the adult collection and what it means to be a women, too.”

This exploration extends into Misha & Puff’s campaign. Roe shared on a phone call that the idea of partnering with Misha & Puff stemmed from just being a fan of the brand. “I said, ‘I don’t know what we can do but I really want to do something with Anna.’ Little did I know that in the background she was working on this unbelievable adult collection,” she said. Though this isn’t the first project Roe has starred in with her daughter, she explained it was the first where she was shot by another mother, making the experience feel truly special—especially as she comes into her body 15 months postpartum. “I feel kind of hot as a mom. There are a lot of narratives out there about getting back to whatever that pre-baby thing is, and I just kind of rebuke that in every single way. I think what I am now is kind of amazing and I really do feel like Mara was able to bring that out in a way that no one else could have.”

On the vision for the campaign, Hoffman shared that the focus was “seeing how does a woman exist through a space or on the street, and how does she live in it?” Working to capture Roe in a documentarian way, the artist wanted to make sure the imagery felt authentic to both the brand and the people wearing it. “We are lucky to be able to capture little shots of that along the way.” Of course, shooting with a baby can come with its own unpredictability. Luckily, as Roe shared, working with someone like Hoffman helped her relax on set with the reminder, “This is just life.”

The seventh annual Kips Bay Decorator Show House in Dallas returns to 2999 Turtle Creek Boulevard, but don’t expect it to look anything like it did in 2025. A new group of the country’s leading designers has taken on the 25,000-square-foot French Renaissance estate, transforming each room to showcase bold ideas, highlight exceptional craftsmanship, and reveal the upcoming trends we can expect to see in the world of interior design.

Visit the show house and see each of the 22 designers’ rooms, from the first dedicated home gym in Kips Bay history by Dallas-based Platinum Gym Design, to a small but mighty European-inspired kitchen by Stephenson Home, to a 1970s-inspired primary bathroom fit with a glass brick shower and curtained-off water closet by Nuance Interiors. With sponsors like Benjamin Moore, The Shade Store, The Rug Company, and more, the vibrant and personality-filled spaces come as no surprise.

As always, proceeds from the show house go to the Kips Bay Boys & Girls Club, which provides educational, enrichment, and developmental programs to thousands of young people, as well as Dallas-based nonprofits Dwell with Dignity and The Crystal Charity Ball.

To see this celebration of exceptional design, you can purchase tickets here and visit the house from Saturday, November 14th to Sunday, December 6th. However, if you can’t make it to the Lone Star State in time, check out some of our favorite moments from the event below.

Kelsi Lamberth of Nuance Interiors pulled inspiration from the 1970s for her primary bathroom, separating the shower from the main prep space using a curved glass brick wall. The sculptural aspects can be found throughout in this groovy space.

In the primary bedroom, Troy Rivington of Rivington Marx Interiors cocooned the room in a dark floral wallpaper and accessorized with other moody botanicals throughout. He was inspired by the romance of 1940s Cairo, dressing the room up like it belonged to a well-traveled collector.

As the first ever dedicated home gym at the Kips Bay Show House, Peter Hoffman of Platinum Gym Design chose a refined, luxurious setup. He named the room Tanren after the Japanese art of hammering and refining metal, and used walnut in both the equipment and the ceiling slats, stainless steel frames, and brown leather accents to complete the exercise space.

In this bespoke bathroom, Russ Peters and Bill Cates of Peters Cates Design lined the wall behind the Studio McGee x Kohler bathtub with a rich merlot tile by RIAD Tile. It’s a beautiful statement and a fabulous way to bring more texture and dimension to the room.

In this tucked away library space, filled with collected finds, designers Christina Garcia Lysaught and Grayson Knight of Layered Dimensions finished off this dark space with a stunning statement mirror. Around the perimeter are resin busts of wildlife, like owls and deer, bringing in a bejeweled touch to the room.

The small but mighty kitchen, designed by Katie Stephenson of Stephenson Home, is crowned with a crackled-gold blooming wallpaper, bringing a warm balance to the rest of the room. It’s covered in birds, butterflies, and blossoms, and it wraps the cook space in a golden glow, reminding all who enter that this room should be as beautiful as it is functional.

The citron paint color wrapping the walls in Jen Bienvenu’s entrance hall is undoubtedly enchanting and serves as the perfect backdrop for her “After the Hunt” theme, but it’s the lampshades made from old silk saris that tie everything together for us. They provide such a magical warmth and really capture the essence of a collector’s treasure room.

Related Story: Almost Every Piece in This Layered Arkansas Home Was a Lucky Antique Find

Step through the citron entry and enter the round room, designed in collaboration by Helen Bergin Interiors and Lichten Architects. The walls are softened by long curtains from The Shade Store, which create beautiful juxtaposition with the curved, sculptural silver media console by Asher Gillman. The actual turntable is flush to the surface, giving it a seamless look while it emits wonderful sound.

In the Withdrawing Room by Jen Stevens of Fonde Interiors, plaster botanicals by artist Amanda Norman come to life as they crawl from the mantel along the chimney breast, escaping to the ceiling. The vines were handmade by Norman and capture the essence of a garden left undisturbed, showing that this formal-at-first-glance room has a wilder side.

The rosy palette in designer Jen Dean’s—founder of Jede Interiors—grand bathroom is topped off with a hand-painted floral mural that covers the ceiling. The rose-gold shine reflects the natural light in the room and give it more depth, while the natural motifs spread across the rest of the space.

Inside this observatory bedroom by sisters Amy Mobley and Katie Norrid of City Hill Design, the Verellen bed is raised up from the ground on a custom platform, emphasizing the importance of the furniture’s role in this space meant for relaxation and rest. It’s wrapped in a striped silk carpet that beckons your touch with a chartreuse mohair sofa at the foot.

Related Story: A Trip to the Lone Star State Inspired the Earthy Textures of This Tennessee New Build

Colorful and collected, this vibrant library by designer Betsy Wentz is not visually quiet. The maximalist space is covered in pattern-mixed Schumacher from ceiling to floor, and the designer pumped up the volume by opting for this triangular table in this tucked away corner.

In designer Amy Switzer’s textural bar lounge—filled with plush chairs, unique artwork, large tassel accessories, and beaded cigarettes—it’s the stone details that really make the room sing. Onyx cornices crown the windows, blue agate inlays decorate the floor, and a banquette which curves around a custom stone and wood table bring a natural coolness to the room that only stone can bring.

#6614. I Walked After Every Meal for Two Months, and My Digestion and Energy Levels Have Never Been Better

Experts weigh in on why sitting is the worst thing you can do after eating

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It’s almost 9:00 p.m., and my work dinner in Manhattan’s SoHo neighborhood is finally coming to a close. As the people around me start to get up and call their Ubers, I head out the door to go home—on foot. After a lavish dinner, most people’s last thought is to get a brisk walk in, but for me, it’s crucial—not to hit a step count or burn calories, but as my version of a digestif, if you will.

My idea to walk after dinner came from a video I saw months ago from a TikTok nutritionist who touted a brisk 10-minute walk after meals as the key to boosting metabolism, regulating blood sugar levels, and helping your stomach digest food. My two favorite pastimes are eating and walking. I never thought the two would go hand in hand.

“Sitting briefly after eating isn’t inherently harmful, but prolonged, uninterrupted sitting can lead to a higher post-meal blood-sugar response compared with breaking it up with short walks,” says Elizabeth Sharp Edens, an internal medicine and obesity medicine physician, functional medicine practitioner, and founder of HMW Method. A 2022 meta-analysis in Sports Medicine found that light-intensity walking reduced post-meal glucose by almost 17 percent. The same study found that standing breaks after meals reduced glucose spikes by 9.5 percent on average. The TL;DR: Research says that any type of movement can improve glucose levels.

We know walking can do wonders—it can clear the mind, help you lean out, and even boost dopamine—but why is it a solution for feeling less full and avoiding afternoon crashes? “When you walk, your muscles use glucose for energy,” Edens explains. “Muscle contractions move glucose transporters called GLUT4 to the surface of muscle cells, helping draw glucose out of the bloodstream through a pathway that doesn’t depend on insulin.” Since your legs, the vehicle for walking, contain some of the biggest muscles in your body, it makes sense that walking effectively stimulates muscle contractions that move glucose transporters. “Walking breaks are a simple way to support blood sugar management while getting your steps in,” she adds.

While many rely on peptides, green powders, and “magic” supplements, walking is an easy, mindless (and free) way to improve digestion and prevent blood-sugar crashes. “Even two to five minutes after a meal can help, ideally before the glucose peak, typically 60 to 90 minutes after eating,” Kiran Krishnan, a research microbiologist, the founder and chief science officer of the Biome Learning Center, and Dose key opinion leader, adds.

I often joke after large meals that I will have to be rolled home. The good news: Walking can also reduce the overwhelming feeling of fullness. “Walking also helps the gut physically,” Krishnan says, citing a study that found that a slow walk after a meal significantly shortened the time it took the stomach to empty half its contents. “For people prone to bloating, mild [walking] cut intestinal gas retention from 45 percent to 24 percent and eased symptoms,” he adds. Plus, Krishnan says studies show reduced LDL cholesterol levels and improved liver function in those who walked after meals.

Then there’s good old gravity, says Caitlin Hosmer, a Maine-based registered dietitian and co-founder of MenoPantry. “Gravity helps too, which is part of why walking may help people who feel uncomfortably full or get reflux after meals,” she explains. “Gentle movement and staying upright help food move out of the stomach and along the digestive tract.”

Ten minutes isn’t long, but studies show it’s just as effective as a longer walk. A 2025 study published by PubMed Central found that a 10-minute walk lowered glucose measurements by 6 percent and a 30-minute walk lowered glucose levels by 5 percent, meaning just 10 minutes of walking is all you need to help reduce a post-meal glucose spike. If you can walk for 30 minutes, an hour, or even longer—that’s great. But just 10 minutes can work just as well.

What matters most is how quickly you get moving. “Glucose typically peaks 60 to 90 minutes after eating, and moving before that peak is what blunts the spike,” Hosmer says. “A walk puts your muscles to work just as glucose from the meal is flooding into the bloodstream.” At first, I questioned whether I had to walk after every meal. “Put your effort where it counts most: after your largest, most carbohydrate-rich meal,” Hosmer advises, adding that for most, that’s after dinner, but walking after all three meals is ideal.

My post-meal walks varied—some days I would walk for 30 minutes or even an hour, depending on how much time I had and where I was going next. But as I started incorporating them into my work schedule, especially on busy office days, I often had only 10 minutes to spare. When in a pinch, I would get up and walk around the office floor and, at home, do air squats, which engage the same large leg muscles as walking and can be just as effective as a post-meal walk.

It may feel strange to pencil in time to walk after every meal, but the benefits I have noticed surpass any inconvenience or awkwardness. I have fewer crashes after I eat, whereas I previously would feel lethargic after every meal. I’ve also noticed improved digestion. While this can be chalked up to a number of things (my beloved vibration plate, greens powders, or digestive enzymes), I always feel lighter and less full after a post-meal walk.

It’s also not meant to feel daunting or like a chore. “Your post-dinner walk isn’t a workout. It’s a way of helping your body handle the meal,” Hosmer says. “The one real ‘wrong way’ is skipping it because you think it has to be long or perfect. I often say something is better than nothing, and that’s especially true here. Even a few minutes of walking, started soon after you finish eating, can blunt the blood sugar rise, and it may help your digestion too.”

#6613. The Miami Heat Dropped Brand-New Jerseys Just in Time for Grand Theft Auto VI

Growing up in Oakland, Miami Heat forward Keshad Johnson and his brother Kenny used to sneak away from their parents to play Grand Theft Auto. “It caused some fights between me and him on turns,” Johnson says. “We used to play that if you crash the car, you gotta pass the sticks.”

For many of us who came of age in the early aughts, sneaking away from our parents to play GTA was a rite of passage. And since the first edition of the game dropped in 1997, at least part of the thrill of this fictional world was often tied to the clandestine affair. But next week, Johnson won’t be hiding from anybody. Instead, he’ll be part of a once-in-a-lifetime Grand Theft Auto experience when he and his Heat teammates take the court in special-edition Vice City jerseys inspired by the game.

Grand Theft Auto VI, Vice City, launches on November 19th. But the night before, when the Heat and superstar Giannis Antetokounmpo take on his former team, the Milwaukee Bucks, they'll be ringing in what is by most accounts the biggest video game launch of all time with a special event that only Rockstar Games and the Heat could pull off. “My whole family is trying to get a Vice City jersey,” Johnson said when we spoke last weekend.

“We're bringing sports and entertainment together in a way that's never been done,” adds Miami Heat Chief Creative Officer Jennifer Alvarez. “And we're going to deliver an experience that no one has actually had at an NBA game.”

More on that in a second. But let’s start with the kits: all black, with bright pink accents that pop like neon signs in the South Beach sky. The word “Heat” is splashed across the front. “It's kind of like the outlaw type vibe,” Johnson said. “That's what we want to give when we're on the court.”

Hidden inside the letters and jersey numbers is a map of Miami streets. They were designed by Nike and Travis Scott’s Cactus Jack, whose logos are featured on the jersey and shorts. As the whole campaign makes clear, details matter.

“I feel like Vice City has its own fashion culture,” says Heat star Bam Adebayo.

The jerseys will be available for purchase on game night at the arena, where fans will be transported into the video game itself upon entering the Kaseya Center, whose plaza will be made over with a Grotti Cheetah and Albany Manana, just two of the sports cars one can drive in GTA.

A sign hoisted atop the arena will read “Welcome to Vice City.” In fact, Mitchell was late to practice one day because his usual route was blocked by a helicopter that’d been deployed to help install it. “It shows how much time and effort they're trying to put into this new game,” Mitchell says. “This is probably gonna be the greatest game of all time.”

Though everyone involved has kept tight-lipped about what happens once inside the arena, fans attending Heat games have already been able to order burgers from Burger Shot and chicken from Cluckin' Bell, two fictional fast-food chains in the Grand Theft Auto universe. “It's a full 360 experience. I can't wait for people to really understand what that means,” Alvarez said, coyly. “And that's all I can say about it.”

One can understand the secrecy, since the Heat’s Vice City takeover has been two years in the making. It all started when Rockstar Games dropped the trailer for Vice City in December 2023. A digital Kaseya Center can be seen in the first 30 seconds.

“When we saw that we were in the trailer, we thought we should figure something out,” Alvarez recalls. “Because we've been synonymous with the word Vice since 2017."

The Heat launched the Miami Vice campaign in 2017 with its acclaimed Original Vice jerseys that set the standard for NBA teams launching City Edition jerseys. Those campaigns went beyond the uniforms and included local activations like custom license plates and a fashion line created in collaboration with local artists. Over the years, the Heat launched five separate Vice jerseys, each campaign expanding on previous ones. Ask those with the Heat, and they’d agree that this latest installment is the biggest one yet. “It feels like all of it built up to this,” Alvarez said.

To be clear, the Heat don’t look at this as an extension of their own Vice line. Rather, this is meant to be as exclusive as any streetwear brand launch. Also, it’s not easy to transport fans into a video game every single night. Go big, then go home.

Meanwhile, Rockstar has infiltrated Miami, turning the city that inspired Vice City into Vice City itself. Burger Shot came to life through a collaboration with Skinny Louie, a local smash-burger joint that has rebranded their brick-and-mortar (and arena) locations for the launch. Rockstar Games has activations throughout the city, including in Downtown, Little Haiti and the famous Wynwood Walls. It’s an Inception-style, video game outside the video game-type thing that crescendos with the Heat game on the eve of the Grand Theft Auto VI launch.

Players got their first look at the jerseys and the campaign during a team meeting in early October. After hours of presentations about business operations, media responsibilities and other team matters, the energy in the room sparked when Alvarez took the microphone and showed the first Vice City slide. The players locked in. A few even stood up and cheered.

Mitchell, for his part, was taken back to his childhood, when he would come home from his grandma’s house and play Grand Theft Auto until it was time for bed. For a while, Mitchell became obsessed, playing GTA while other popular games like Call of Duty and NBA 2K collected dust.

“I just played that all the time, doing missions, but also just running around,” he remembers. “It's kind of like your own world in a way.”

And next week, he’ll get to enter it IRL.

#6610. We Tested Luxury Sheet Sets for Three Years—These Are the Only Ones Worth the Splurge

For hot sleepers, restless sleepers, and anyone tired of scratchy bedding.

#6608. Understated, Earthy, and Endlessly Wearable: The Best Olive Green Polishes

The earthy shade adds an edge to fall manicures while still wearing like a neutral.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Like all nail polish colors, green has a vast spectrum, one that runs from electric neon to bold kelly to soft sage and all the way down to deep, moody olive. Of all the greens out there, olive sits in a quieter place. The hue is earthy and a little mysterious, somewhere between a vintage army jacket and an actual juicy olive. It’s a shade we love for fall, since it pairs so seamlessly with black, rich browns, burgundy, red, and, of course, cream.

Once reserved for the brave few, olive has now gone mainstream. Part of the appeal is how wearable it is, offering an unexpected twist without ever feeling too loud. It’s also soft and soothing to the eye, making it an easy shade to wear day after day.

If you’re new to the shade, the easiest way in is to treat it like a neutral. Try it with a camel coat and chunky knits when the weather turns, or a crisp white shirt for something fresh and unexpected. A creamy, opaque finish feels polished and modern, while a glossy jelly or a hint of shimmer adds depth in low light. However you wear it, olive looks effortlessly considered and adds an edge to your style.

Below, we’ve rounded up the best olive green nail polishes to shop now.

A personal favorite, Elia is a muted olive green that looks rich from the very first stroke. The opaque formula glides on evenly in a single swipe and dries to a soft gloss that lasts through daily wear.

Manucurist’s take on olive green feels a touch brighter. It sits beautifully on light and dark skin tones alike and delivers an opaque wash of color. Part of the “Green Flash” collection, it cures under an LED gel lamp and lasts for nearly 21 days.

Essie’s Totally Plaid is an olive green polish with a cream finish that delivers a gel-like shine and depth while still removing as easily as a regular polish. The formula applies smoothly in two coats, giving you rich, opaque color without the need for a UV lamp.

This deep and moody olive green shade is the epitome of effortless chic, pairing easily with everything from neutral knits to bold jewel tones.

Inspired by the lush landscapes of the Mediterranean, this olive green evokes a lighter take on the olive color spectrum. It’s a tad brighter and slightly more yellow-toned, making it a great pick if you want a fresh, sunlit green this fall.

O.P.I’s Suzi is the chic olive green and wardrobe staple of the olive family. It’s a bit darker-toned, radiating earthy warmth and understated elegance. Plus, it’s fast-drying and offers up to seven days of wear.

For those seeking a little more sparkle, this olive green jelly is packed with large green holographic glitters that create a textured finish and catch the light with every movement, adding a spark of joy to your manicure.

Calming and serene, this moss green shade is part of the “Campground Collection”, a four-shade assortment of earthy, comforting colors. Its buttery-smooth application matches the shade’s peaceful look.

This may not look like your average olive green at first glance, but that’s because it has taupe undertones. Once it’s on your nails, you’ll notice the hint of green was there all along. The result is a soft, grounded neutral that pairs effortlessly with cozy fall knits and earthy accessories.

This nail color may be named Pickle, but we see the olive in there. This tangy green with muted yellow undertones feels lively while remaining neutral enough to pair with everything in your wardrobe.

A true olive green, Extra Dirty brings rich, earthy depth to your nails. All you need is one to two coats for a creamy manicure worthy of a fall-season spotlight.

#6607. I Own 400 Sneakers. You Should Only Own 21

I own far too many sneakers. There are everyday beaters, rare samples, and plenty in between, accumulated over more than a decade of collecting. That’s a lot of shoes by any reasonable measure. Around 400 at my last count. A few of my favorites took some work to get. I entered a stupid number of raffles for the JJJJound x New Balance 990v3, lined up overnight for the Sacai x Nike VaporWaffle, and caved and paid resale for the Gucci x Adidas Gazelle.

With that many pairs, you start thinking about what actually earns its space. A shoe can be interesting to collect and difficult to wear. Another can seem almost too obvious to buy, then turn out to be the thing that works with most of your clothes. If I could wipe the slate clean, I’d pay much more attention to that second category. I’d still want some fun stuff, obviously. I’m rebuilding a sneaker collection, not writing a packing list.

So, where would I start? With these 21 pairs from Foot Locker’s selection. There are basketball shoes I’d want for their shape and history, runners I’d buy for everyday wear, and a few low-profile pairs to switch things up. Some are famous enough that they barely need an introduction. But knowing a shoe’s name and knowing why you’d want it in your collection are different things. Here’s why these would make it back into mine.

Yes, four of my first five picks are Nike or Jordan – and that’s deliberate. If I were rebuilding my collection, they’d still get a big chunk of my budget. The Air Jordan 1, Air Force 1, and Dunk are a pretty good explanation for why. If you’re starting with jeans and a tee, I’d look here first. A high-top gives you a little more shoe around the ankle. A low-top is easier with shorts, and white Forces can do a lot of the work when you’re getting dressed in a hurry.

I’d start right here, before getting distracted by anything limited to 200 pairs. Peter Moore’s 1985 design gets the shape so right: the height of the collar, the panels around the toe, the way contrasting colors divide up the upper. The High OG also gives you the Nike Air tongue branding. I want a pair that looks good with straightforward jeans and a tee, and the Air Jordan 1 has been perfecting that combo for decades.

A fresh white Air Force 1 would be an early purchase for the deeply boring reason that I’d wear it constantly. Bruce Kilgore’s 1982 basketball silhouette has enough weight to sit properly under loose jeans, and that beefy sole gives the whole fit a little more presence. White-on-white also makes the leather panels and perforations easier to appreciate. It’s the pair I’d reach for when I like everything else I’m wearing and don’t need to complicate things.

Once you’ve looked at enough Dunks, you notice how much the colorblocking changes the sneaker. Its college basketball background gave those panels a specific purpose: carrying team colors. The ‘Sanded Purple’ makes good use of that layout. I’d want a Dunk Low because the shape is uncomplicated enough to wear regularly, while the colors give an outfit a clear starting point. Pick up one of those shades elsewhere, or leave the rest nice and neutral.

The Superstar arrived as a basketball shoe in 1970; Run-D.M.C.’s “My Adidas” helped give it a very different audience in 1986. That history is good to know, but the Shelltoe is what would get my money. It gives the front of the shoe a distinctive shape, and the Superstar II’s extra padding makes the whole thing feel chunkier than the OG. I’d put these under straight jeans, with enough of the toe showing to appreciate it.

The High would come first, of course, but I’d still make room for an Air Jordan 1 Low OG. Removing the tall collar changes how the panels sit with your pants, giving you more space around the ankle and a less bulky-looking sneaker. I’d buy it for days when I want that familiar Jordan colorblocking with shorts or slightly shorter pants. There’s enough difference to justify the second box.

For a day with a lot of walking, I’d start with the 990v6 or the Zoom Vomero 5. There are plenty of ways to get that mesh running-shoe look, and the XT-6 is the one I’d pick if I wanted a trail sole with more grip.

Yes, there would absolutely be gray New Balances in the rebuild. The 990 family started in 1982, but the sixth-gen adds FuelCell cushioning and lets the suede overlays flow across the mesh without the usual midfoot saddle. You can see the difference, and there’s a practical benefit underfoot, too. This is the pair I’d buy for days with a lot of walking: comfy enough to justify the purchase, good-looking enough that comfort isn’t the only justification.

The OG 2008 Gel-Kayano 14 was the first in the series designed by someone other than Toshikazu Kayano – useful information for your next deeply specific sneaker convo. More relevant here is how well the layered mesh and synthetic overlays work together. The ‘Graphite Grey’ has enough contrast to show off the construction, with Gel cushioning right underneath.

The 1906R is for when I want all the little technical details. Open mesh, curvy overlays, and segmented cushioning around the heel give you plenty to check out, especially in white, silver, and black. It shares the same sole tech with the 2002R and 860v2, but the upper just looks more put-together.

The Zoom Vomero 5 launched back in 2011, but it didn’t gain its cult following until about a decade later. There’s a lot to enjoy up top: open mesh, overlapping panels, and plastic caging that becomes particularly obvious in ‘Metallic Silver’. Zoom Air cushioning gives it a practical role in the collection, too. I’d buy this as a regular-wear pair for long days, with enough detail to make jeans and a plain sweater look put together.

First released in 2010, the Omni 9 has all the mesh and supporting structure you’d expect from a running shoe of that era. This white and pink version lets you see how the layers fit together, with ProGrid cushioning underneath. I’d want it because a collection can become very repetitive once you find a couple of brands you like. The Omni gives me another interpretation of the technical runner, with enough character to earn its place alongside the Nikes and Asics.

The P-6000 looks like a straight archive reissue, but it actually combines elements from the Pegasus 25 and Pegasus 2006. I’d buy the white and silver combo and wear the hell out of them – every pair doesn’t need to be an occasion.

The XT-6 started life in 2013 as a serious trail running shoe, and you can still see that purpose in the reinforced upper, Quicklace system, and lugged outsole. My plans would probably involve considerably less altitude. I’d buy it because the close-fitting upper and outdoor construction bring something different to the collection, particularly with cargo pants or wider-leg pants. The ‘Black Coffee’ also makes it easy to wear with denim, olive, and navy. No hiking itinerary required.

If your jeans taper or you like a shorter hem, try something that sits closer to the foot. The Samba is an easy place to start in black leather. I’d go for the green Spezial if I wanted a little color without having to think too hard about the rest of the fit.

Collecting can make you weird about buying something that everybody else owns – I’d try to avoid that with the Samba. Its roots go back to soccer shoes for icy fields in 1950, but the slim shape is what earns it a place here. After a few chunky basketball shoes, you need something that sits closer to the foot. ‘Core Black’ leather, white stripes, and a suede T-toe give you plenty to work with, particularly under a straighter pair of pants.

Yes, there’s already a Samba here. The Handball Spezial earns its own place with its rounded toe, suede upper, and gum sole, which give it a softer appearance than the leather-heavy pairs. First made for handball players in 1979, it’s also a good way to bring some color into the rebuild. The green and white do enough on their own. I’d wear these with blue jeans and let the suede take care of the rest.

The Gazelle dates back to 1966, making this year its 60th birthday. I’d buy it for the suede upper and the straightforward proportions, which give it a slightly different feel from the other Adidas silhouettes here. In black and white, it’s easy to wear with faded denim or dark pants. Some days, a familiar shape in simple colors is exactly what you want.

Puma’s Suede history runs back to 1968, so I’d want some of that history in the collection, as well as the shoe’s simple construction. The soft upper and sweeping Formstrip give you texture and shape without a bunch of extra panels. It would be a useful change after several technical runners, especially with denim or cotton pants that already have plenty of texture themselves.

Wide jeans and heavier layers can take a bigger shoe. I’d look at the Air Max 95 for the layered upper, the Gel-NYC if I wanted something a little quieter, or the 9060 if I wanted the sole to do most of the talking.

Sergio Lozano was inspired by human anatomy for the Air Max 95, translating ribs, muscle fibers, and a spine into a running shoe. A pretty weird design concept that produced a very good sneaker. Those layered side panels are the reason I’d buy it again: they give the shoe depth even in this low-key black, white, and gray combination. It has enough bulk for wider pants, and enough going on that the rest of the fit can stay simple.

The Gel-NYC looks pretty old school, but Asics actually assembled it from several archive references. There’s Gel-Nimbus 3 and Gel-MC Plus V in the upper, with Gel-Cumulus 16 tooling underneath. The result has a fuller shape than the Kayano, with more emphasis on those broad suede panels. That’s why I’d make room for both. This ‘Cream’ and ‘Oyster Grey’ version works particularly well beneath wider pants, where a very slim shoe can disappear under the hem.

A collection of completely sensible sneakers would feel like an opportunity missed. The 9060 takes details from New Balance’s 99X family and blows them up: the 990’s sway bars spread across the upper, while the sole gets a sculpted, pod-like shape. I’d pick this brown version to balance out bigger pants and heavier layers. It gives those clothes a chunky enough shoe to sit over.

These are the two I’d happily get dirty. Go for the Chucks if you like a high-top with cuffed jeans, or the Old Skools if you want something low that’s just as easy to wear with shorts.

Black canvas Chucks would be back on the shelf pretty quickly, too. Their basketball DNA stretches all the way back to 1917, but it’s the narrow shape I’d want in this collection. It gives jeans a completely different finish from an AF1 or a 990, especially with a little ankle showing. These are also shoes I’d be happy to wear until the canvas softened and the rubber picked up some marks.

To finish off my new collection, I’d grab a pair of Old Skools. Launched in 1977 as the Style 36, it introduced the Jazz Stripe along the way. The canvas-and-suede upper, white stripe, and waffle sole are still enough to make it worth owning. It looks good with jeans, works with shorts, and improves once the upper loosens up. After all the comparing and researching and rebuilding, I’d want at least one pair I could put on and forget about.

#6606. Florence Pugh Puts a Sculptural Twist on Victorian Mourning Dressing for an East of Eden Event

She gave new meaning to the term power shoulders

The East of Eden method dressing isn’t over yet. Last night, the cast of Netflix’s limited drama series returned to the red carpet for a FYC (“For Your Consideration”) event in Los Angeles, California. And for the occasion, Florence Pugh embraced the story’s time period with a sculptural, Victorian look with over-the-top power shoulders.

Designed by Harris Reed, the ensemble echoed classic Victorian mourning dressing, a custom popularized by Queen Victoria after the 1861 death of her husband, Prince Albert. (Just one year before the first chapter of East of Eden takes place.) The modest style required all-black fabrics, high necklines, and long sleeves—all of which can be seen in Pugh’s tailored peplum jacket, with its V-notch stand collar and fabric-covered buttons. Of course, the actor’s version modernized the concept, with exaggerated puff sleeves that demanded attention.

Stylist Rebecca Corbin-Murray paired the look with platform heels and Bulgari jewels, once again breaking the traditional dress code, and hair stylist Adir Abergel gave Pugh’s blonde locks a messy updo. Makeup artist Alex Babsky finished things off with a moody deep-red lipstick, a custom shade he mixed together himself.

Pugh was joined by co-star Christopher Abbott and series creator Zoe Kazan, who adapted John Steinbeck’s 1952 novel for the screen. The Little Women actor not only starred in the 2026 interpretation, but also served as executive producer. She brought a nuanced performance to the role of Cathy, who has traditionally been seen as a soulless antagonist, but here was given a more complex, compelling backstory that humanized her.

#6604. The Latest Look at Taylor Swift’s Off-Duty Style Comes With a New Detail About Her Wedding

Taylor Swift has flown under the radar for most of the fall, only making public appearances at her husband Travis Kelce’s home games and a few industry events. Yesterday, however, fans got a new look at Swift’s casual, off-duty style in an unexpected place: the Hancock County Humane Foundation’s Instagram. The animal welfare nonprofit shared a photo of Swift and Kelce with Kelce’s longtime agent, Mike Simon, and his wife Lisa Marie, who attended their wedding. The post revealed a new detail about the newlyweds’ request to guests in lieu of giving them gifts.

“Four beautiful people, four generous hearts,” the West Virginia-based organization wrote. “The Hancock County Humane Foundation is honored to acknowledge a very generous donation from Attorney Mike Simon and his wife Lisa in honor of a very special wedding they recently attended. The amazing bride and groom asked for donations to charities in lieu of gifts and Mike and Lisa chose us!!”

Swift appeared to be wearing the red Tommy Hilfiger cable-knit polo she wore during Kelce’s game on Sunday with baggy, light-wash jeans.

The post came hours after The Hollywood Reporter revealed Swift would be receiving the Sherry Lansing Leadership Award at its Women in Entertainment Gala. Greta Gerwig will present the honor to her, which “recognizes trailblazers and philanthropists in entertainment and media and was established in honor of Sherry Lansing, the first woman to head a Hollywood studio,” the outlet wrote.

“Taylor Swift took on an industry that has long underestimated women and won on every front: artistically, commercially, and on the question of who owns her work,” the publication’s editor-in-chief, Maer Roshan, said. “She reclaimed her catalog, set new terms for the artists who follow her, and became the most popular musician in the world while doing it—and helping scores of other artists along the way. We’re proud to honor her with the Sherry Lansing Leadership Award.”

#6602. Zimmermann Hosts a Star-Studded Soirée in Downtown New York City

Katie Holmes, Uma Thurman, and Naomi Watts came out to celebrate the brand’s cruise 2027 collection.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Inside Indochine’s red-lit, retro-inspired French-Vietnamese dining room in New York City, Zimmermann gathered friends of the brand to celebrate its cruise 2027 collection. Presented on the sun-drenched Côte d’Azur in June, the label’s latest served as the perfect bit of vacation and occasion-ready dressing for November in New York. Now that the lineup has officially hit stores, fashion insiders and fans of the brand alike (including Uma Thurman, Eve Hewson, Katie Holmes, and Naomi Watts) showed up dripping in ruffled gowns, sailor-inspired stripes, chunky shearlings, and ethereal lace and silks from the collection. Against the dark, 1940s-inspired tropical salon interior of Indochine, it was the ideal mix of downtown energy and New York glamour.

As champagne flowed through the bar area, glasses clinked while miniature crab cakes and spring rolls were passed. Zimmermann’s sister duo Nicky and Simone Zimmermann could be spotted catching up with friends new and old. “We have a very, very close connection with New York,” Nicky told ELLE in between greeting guests. “It was pretty much when I started the business, one of the first places internationally that I went to in the ’90s, and it blew my mind. It’s been inspirational to us 100 percent.” It was a rare occasion for the brand; for years, Zimmermann has shown at Paris Fashion Week (after presenting in New York in the mid-2010s) and the duo oscillates between Sydney and Paris for most of the year.

Zimmermann’s painterly and intrinsically bohemian flourishes could be seen in the many outfits of guests, all highlighting the vivid cruise collection. Think: decadent silky draped drop-waisted gowns and paneled lace maxi dresses, or, for the more demure, sleek all-black looks that captured the New York essence. “For me, there’s a little bit of a sense of humor behind it—without insulting anybody—it was about the story when Australia actually beat America in the America’s Cup, which is a very famous sailing race,” Nicky told ELLE of the collection’s inspiration.

“I think it was in 1983, and America had not lost the America’s Cup in something like 173 years; it was a ridiculous winning streak, and Australia came along. The inspiration is more about a David and Goliath kind of story,” she continued. “We came along as the Aussies, not established in the sailing world. They were very cheeky, rogue, kind of Aussie young guys up against this amazing, sophisticated establishment of the New York Yacht Club. And they never lost—and we beat them. So in Australia, it’s a legendary story.” Nicky combined the sportiness of sailing gear with the sort of elite New York Yacht Club preppiness, resulting in colorful silk scarf embellishment or sweaters decked out in accessorized pins. “They would hold the most incredible parties and the women were so glamorous and sophisticated and beautiful and not anything that Australia could relate to at the time, so I loved the contrast.”

Conversation was flowing and blooming anthuriums covered the tables as guests took their seats. Nicky kicked off the dinner with a speech, musing on her early days in New York on the Lower East Side and the many parties she attended in Tribeca before sharing more inspiration behind the collection: “It’s about establishment, and then it’s about people, you know, working really hard, coming together as a team, defeating the undefeatable,” she said, with a laugh.

Next came an intimate performance by the singer and Bad Monkey actress Charlotte Lawrence, who sang two of her original songs, then led a folksy sing-along to “Dreams” by Fleetwood Mac. Even the most guarded of celebs and fashion’s elite couldn’t help but bob their heads and sing a tune. As guests dined on a family-style mix of kale salad, spicy shrimp, grilled salmon, barbecued chicken, and steak, the champagne glass clinks slowed as candles slowly flickered and the evening closed out with lemon tarts.

A little yacht-club polish, a little Aussie irreverence: Zimmermann celebrated cruise 2027 in high style.

#6601. The Best Oxford Shirt for Men in 2026, According to GQ

The story behind the Oxford shirt is a lot less thrilling than you’d expect. It didn’t earn that fancy-sounding sobriquet through some sacred connection to the tony British university; instead, the shirt's signature cotton fabric was just one of four named after a group of schools picked by a Scottish mill for their associations with society’s upper crust. (19th century marketing at its best!)

But of the quartet—the others were Harvard, Cambridge, and Yale, FYI—only the Oxford shirt achieved menswear icon status, becoming a quintessential emblem of American prep as a “sporting shirt” and then as a staple of casual attire. Nowadays, Oxford-cloth shirts come in every color imaginable, but none of ‘em look quite as classic as the OG—especially when they’re thoroughly worn-in and a little wrinkled. Below you’ll find 16 of our absolute favorites, each one more ready than the last to imbue your jeans, chinos, and trousers with the unmistakable swagger of adopted American royalty.

J.Crew’s Oxford shirts have been a staple of the catalog for decades and though its iconic Secret Wash shirts are the bestsellers of the bunch, we prefer its more recent release, the 1983 Oxford Shirt. It’s easy to miss the differences at a glance, yet the handful of subtle tweaks add up quick. First, the fit: a comfier, more relaxed silhouette that, despite its ‘80s reference, is spot on for 2027. Second, the fabric: a noticeably sturdier, heftier all-cotton Oxford that makes its best-selling Secret Wash shirts feel wimpy by comparison. Third, and most importantly, the collar: unlike its most popular shirts, the 1983 Oxford has a satisfyingly taller collar with a prep-approved collar roll. It gives the shirt more life and more nuance, but also looks great under a blazer.

If there’s any brand that could do the Oxford justice, it’s the British label, Drake’s, known for its none-too-posh take on all things tailoring. Its handsome entry into the Oxford shirt ring is a confluence of top-shelf materials and methodical construction, wrapped into a single shirt worth saving up for. Handmade in Somerset, England, Drake’s Oxford features single-needle construction with finished seams throughout, which takes the cut and sew process twice as long to complete—on top of the high-density stitching you’ll find throughout the shirt. Lustrous mother-of-pearl buttons make for a luxe upgrade while the collar—a button-down with a fabulous collar roll—is constructed with a floating interlining to give it a soft structure.

All in, Drake’s Oxford is what most other Oxfords aspire to be. And if you’re curious about what comes after J.Crew, this is your answer.

Wythe’s built its brand on western aesthetics with lasting quality—think properly-made cowboy boots, Yellowstone-worthy coats, and snap shirts. That the label would produce something as east-coast as an Oxford shirt is head-scratching. And yet, it’s one of the best versions we’ve tried. That’s because Wythe takes the same sort of rigor that it uses for its western and workwear garments and applies it to the preppy classic. This as close as anyone can get to a deadstock Oxford shirt plucked from a long-forgotten storage room. From the box pleat and locker loop to the unstructured long-point button-down collar, size-stamped collar stand and nostalgic paper packaging, it’s a good reminder of why prep in the ‘60s was so, so good.

Plain Oxford shirts too simple for your liking? Thom Browne's take isn’t overtly avant-garde, but it does boast a striped grosgrain placket that shows itself when you undo the top or bottom buttons, a stitched-on tag near the right hip, and a similarly striped locker loop beneath the collar. Each one is made in Italy from a soft, durable cotton fabric with noticeable cuffs and a sharply curved hem, making this iteration a better fit with sleek dress pants or even your most refined athleisure. (Talking to you, sneakers-with-suit crowd.)

This shirt won’t win you any browny points with the tailoring nerds, it will earn you cred with the fashion elite.

For the guy who’s quick to chat your ear off for 20 minutes when all you said was, “nice pants”, Jake’s is the go-to shirt whisperer. Jake’s began as founder Jake Wigham was amidst his studies at the London College of Fashion, honing his skills at a tailoring apprenticeship and fulfilling custom projects. It eventually blossomed into the talk of the menswear cognoscenti, who praised Wigham’s shirtmaking prowess. Each shirt is made-to-order, cut and sewn in the Jake’s studio by a small team of expert craftspeople, according to your specific measurements, with options for different collars, pockets, and fabrics. While we’ll always respect the old guard shirtmakers who’ve honed their style over generations, Jake’s bridges the gap between traditional craft and modern appeal—a Savile Row approach that speaks internet.

According to menswear lore, Brooks Brothers is responsible for bringing the Oxford shirt stateside. Quite a few decades later, everything’s still here, from the telltale collar to the button cuffs, patch pockets, and curved hems. One note: Brooks Brothers says it’s a ‘regular fit’, but there’s a bit more room in the chest than some of its counterparts.

Japan's obsession with Americana often comes full circle, as is the case with Kamakura. Its shirts are the envy of so many labels for its craftsmanship which parallels that of custom shirtmakers. We're talking mother-of-pearl buttons, high-density stitching, and major attention to minor details like the roll of the collar and single-needle seams.

Gitman Vintage's stateside-produced shirts have been a fixture of tasteful menswear shops for years not only for its high quality control, but for its tailored silhouettes and idiosyncratic details like chalk buttons, its signature contrasting horizontal bottom button hole, and soft collars.

J.Press's take on the Oxford shirt stands out as among the preppiest examples. Not only does it come from the storied uniform supplier of Yale's student body, but the perfectly rolled collar and flap chest pocket details give it a distinctly collegiate look that would pass muster on any Ivy League campus.

The Clark shirt is one of Proper Cloth's best selling shirts thanks to its beefy Oxford cloth material, bewilderingly good construction (felled seams, split yoke, unfused placket, shanked buttons), and near-perfect fit. For $125, you cannot get a better Oxford shirt. But you have to be willing to wait because every shirt is made to order and will take a couple weeks to get to you. If you can remember to think ahead and have some patience, it’s well worth the wait.

Swedish brand Rubato crafts its R Oxford less traditionally, but it’s no less an Oxford because of it. It might eschew the conventional button-down collar, but thanks its super-tight blue stripes, button cuffs, and a fitted body designed to look good tucked or untucked, it skews decidedly old-world. The real clincher though, is the fabric, a 100% Sea Island cotton so soft we keep trying to pet our computer screen.

With a nerd-satisfying 22 stitches per inch, troca shell buttons, and other refined details, you’d be forgiven for thinking this shirt was made on Jermyn Street, famed for its shirtmaking history. But Sid’s shirts are proudly made in Honduras which makes them a great value compared to the British alternative.

Todd Snyder's lightweight Oxford shirt takes the OG and makes it even more casual, a perfect piece for layering over a graphic tee thanks to its relaxed fit and feather-light cotton fabric.

The quality of an Oxford shirt comes down to the fabric, construction, fit, and collar. They’re a distinct kind of button-up that warrants its own buying guide separate from dress shirts. Why? There’s so much history behind the style and the fabric.

Oxford cloth is beefier than a typical dress shirt fabric with more texture and thus has a more casual quality befitting of rumpled chinos and sneakers, territory most dress shirt fabrics would feel absolutely out of place. Seph Skerritt, CEO of Proper Cloth, says “You can think of it as a tougher, more durable and more casual cousin to the pinpoint dress shirt.” The cotton yarns are thicker than broadcloth, twill, and poplin, so the hand is noticeably less fine. The heftier material means a high-quality Oxford cloth is more durable and can even last as long as a decade.

Construction-wise, you should typically look for the same sort of details as you would with other dress shirts. Clean stitches, felled seams, buttons properly sewn with shanks, and reinforced at the side seams. High-quality Oxford shirts will also feature a split yoke which is the panel that spans the shoulders and is cut on the bias to give the area natural stretch for ease of motion.

Fit is subjective, of course, but you want to make sure that the shoulder seams line up with your natural shoulders, if not a little below for a relaxed fit. The chest shouldn’t pull, but shouldn’t feel like a potato sack. As for the body, this is more or less subjective and delves into the kind of silhouette you’re after, but if the fabric is pulling around the buttons, your shirt is too tight. And, depending on whether you like to tuck, should be long enough.

Oxford cloth shirts can come in any variety of collars, but the most common are button-down, spread, and point collars. Big menswear nerds will obsess over finding the perfect collar roll, a detail found in the golden age of Ivy style by the likes of Brooks Brothers and J.Press.

Oxford shirts are near and dear to our hearts. They’re classic, versatile, and durable—true staples that every guy should have. So we had opinions on what we wanted out of them. It all starts with the star of the show—the titular fabric. The Oxford cloth has to be meatier than the average dress shirt and with some noticeable texture. They should ideally be able to rumple more than crease and wrinkle.

From there, we looked for Oxfords that are well-constructed with beautiful buttons and, crucially, handsome collars. And because you can be surprised no matter how much you’re paying, we looked at Oxfords in all price points to find the best ones regardless of the tag.

So we looked to the seasoned veterans that built the Oxford’s reputation as well as the newcomers that are pushing it into the 21st-century as well as the runway designers that have let their imaginations run wild.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)
