#6599. Culture Watch: What to See and Where to Go in November

Culture Watch is a series spotlighting the intersection of fashion and art, bringing you the latest must-see exhibitions, pop-ups, installations, and more.

November is a good month to make a little room in your calendar. As the holiday season starts to gather pace, galleries, brands, and creative spaces are offering plenty of reasons to get out and look around. In New York, Salon Art + Design returns for its 15th year, while Loro Piana presents its “Master of Cashmere” installation at The Brant Foundation; farther afield, international exhibitions offer even more to explore. Check out all of this month’s best cultural happenings below.

Louis Vuitton Presents ‘La Valise Bruno Aveillan’ at LV Dream

For 13 years, photographer and filmmaker Bruno Aveillan has taken his Louis Vuitton Alzer suitcase to more than 100 destinations, making it a recurring presence in his work. Now, the well-traveled case is at the center of “La Valise Bruno Aveillan,” an immersive exhibition at LV Dream, the house’s encompassing destination in Paris. Aveillan’s photographs appear alongside historic Louis Vuitton trunks and a closer look at the craftsmanship behind the Alzer, the brand’s hard-sided suitcase built around a sturdy wooden frame. The exhibition marks the final chapter in the house’s yearlong celebration of the monogram’s 130th anniversary.

Loro Piana Names Its Cashmere of the Year and Unveils a ‘Master of Cashmere’ Installation

Loro Piana put cashmere in the spotlight at The Brant Foundation in New York, where it marked the 11th edition of its Cashmere of the Year Award. Established in 2015 and held stateside for the first time, the prize recognizes the herders who produce the finest cashmere fiber. Coinciding with the honor, which went to three couples of cashmere herders from Inner Mongolia, is “Master of Cashmere: The Quest for Fiber Excellence,” an installation that traces the material from its origins to the Maison’s work with it. The multi-room experience features archival sketches, explanatory timelines, and, of course, soft-to-the-touch cashmere.

Salon Art + Design Returns to the Park Avenue Armory for Its 15th Year

The 15th edition of Salon Art + Design is now on view at the Park Avenue Armory—and it’s one of its most immersive, expansive editions yet. As is tradition, the event brings together collectible design, fine art, and jewelry. The event is open through November 8. Standouts include Jean Dunand’s 1929 La Forêt lacquered screen, Michel Dufet’s 1918 daybeds, and Jean Royère’s illuminated desk. Fernando Mastrangelo’s totem lamps add a sculptural note, while the jewelry lineup includes pieces from Fernando Jorge, Mellerio, Cora Sheibani, and Viltier.

Lara Saget Debuts Her First New York Solo Show, ‘And the World Came Apart’

Lara Saget brings more than a decade of material experimentation to her first solo exhibition in New York. At Trotter&Sholer’s new Elizabeth Street space, her sculptures and wearable works fuse glass, stone, and metal through heat, pressure, and time. Drawing on geological processes and NASA data, the show moves from ancient natural formations to humanity’s rapid impact on the planet.

The Phillips Collection Opens ‘Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea’

Milton Avery went to Gloucester, Massachusetts, to “live like an artist,” then brought Adolph Gottlieb and Mark Rothko along for summers of creative exchange. In Washington, D.C., The Phillips Collection’s “Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea” brings together watercolors and color-drenched canvases, tracing what those Cape Ann days set in motion.

Tate St Ives Spotlights Wilhelmina Barns-Graham

What does a landscape feel like in the body? Scottish artist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham spent eight decades exploring that question through art shaped by sensation and memory. The retrospective at Tate St Ives in Cornwall, England, is the most comprehensive survey of her work, moving from early landscapes and studio interiors to later works alive with bold color and sweeping gestures.

Taylor Swift, take note: famously hard-to-get-into New York City hotspot The Corner Store has officially landed at The Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas, marking its first-ever location outside Manhattan. Expect its adventurous martinis, signature wood-paneled interiors by Rockwell Group, and a handful of Vegas-exclusive menu additions, including a Butcher’s Counter serving up wagyu tomahawk and porterhouse steaks.

#6598. King Charles Celebrates His 78th Birthday With Elton John

The two talked modern music, the King’s Trust, and more

The king is officially 78! Charles III, who was born in 1948—just four years before his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, took the throne—celebrated another trip around the sun today. And while the official birthday celebration of the monarch falls in June with the annual Trooping the Colour military parade, the royal family marked his real date of birth with a new portrait of him and Sir. Elton John.

The photo was taken during the taping of a special edition of John’s Apple Music 1 radio show, Rocket Hour, in which the “Tiny Dancer” musician was joined by Charles to mark 50 years of the King’s Trust charity. And in addition to discussing the nonprofit, the two also chatted about modern music, introduced over a dozen hand-selected tracks, and joked about aging.

“We and the Trust are definitely still standing,” the king teased, highlighting the Grammy-winning singer’s “I’m Still Standing” as one of his favorite songs. The musician, from his seat at the table, replied, “I’m still sitting now, though.”

At one point, the monarch gave a particular shoutout to Raye, who he said he “had the pleasure of being introduced to” during a “very memorable performance” at Apple.

A key focus of the Rocket Hour podcast has been to champion emerging artists—a mission that resonates with the King’s Trust’s focus on supporting the next generation. Formerly known as the Prince’s Trust, the organization was founded in 1976 to help young people facing unemployment, homelessness, academic troubles, and more. John has celebrated the charity’s milestones before, even performing at Wembley Arena for the 10th anniversary (1986). In 2001, he joined the royal family for a 25th anniversary dinner at St. James’s Palace in London.

“We are so richly blessed with the talents of our musicians, singers, and performers, particularly yourself, if I may say so,” the king continued, turning to his host. “You’ve become such a national treasure.”

#6597. A New Marni x Hoka Sneaker Is Here—Here’s What to Know

The Italian fashion house once again brings its unique touch to the athletic brand.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Last year, when Marni and Hoka launched their first collaboration, the two labels came together to bring the world a collection of puffy, chunky, candy-colored takes on the athletic footwear brand’s Bondi sneaker. Naturally, it was a hit among the streetwear set, including the likes of Steph Curry. Of course, a lot can change in the span of a year and a half—and the latest sneaker trends are no exception. In the same way jeans have gone from baggy styles to straight-leg and even skinny jeans, fashion has taken its sneakers from their dad eras to silhouettes that lean a little sleeker. The latest result of these turning tides: The Hoka Clifton Marni.

“Shifting from the maximalist and oversized aesthetic towards a calmer, more essential form made sense with Meryll [Rogge]’s ascension to Marni,” Thomas Cykana, Hoka’s senior director of global collaborations, tells ELLE in an email. “This affords a simple but surprising design that cues premium embellishments, metallic hardware, and unexpected prints over an overtly in-your-face design. This shift enables consumers to both craft their uniform and express their individuality without sacrificing Hoka’s pure performance capabilities.”

Available now, the design is the culmination of form and function. Marni brings its unique design perspective to the technical shoe, not only with the chosen colors—Orange, Black, and White—but also with design-forward touches such as woven heel tabs, windowpane-patterned insoles, and three shoelace options for each colorway.

“Marni has a unique ability to take everyday design cues and make them feel artful and unexpected. That lust for curiosity and imaginative nature is what first drew our team to the label and continues to inspire us,” Cykana shares. “Our debut collection in 2025 showed how much our teams share in creativity and craftsmanship, and that trust led us to our unique spin on the iconic Clifton. The editorial tone they delivered to this project reflects the perfect sensation of everyday and extraordinary at once.”

#6596. Haven and Converse Made One of the Coolest Chucks of the Year

As perfect as the Converse Chuck Taylor is, that hasn’t stopped the OG sneaker brand from pushing the sneaker's limits through countless collaborations that remake the classic Chucks in a million different images. While most of those collabs tend to be flashier, there are a few that stand out for their restraint. Or at least, what appears to be restraint at first glance. After a sellout partnership, Canadian outfitters and tastemakers Haven have reunited with Converse for its second team-up, lifting the vaunted Chuck 70 to new heights.

Haven’s disciplined approach to design considers its roots in Vancouver, the topography and climes therein, and incorporates that into its garments. Think waterproof shells, lightweight insulation, gussets for range of motion. “We think about the real world. What do you actually need to wear and what do you need to make you comfortable, and how to make your day a little bit better,” Haven cofounder Arthur Chmielewski says. “It could be just 1 per cent better. But those little details over time, they make your life a little bit better, right?” But it’s not just optimizing in the most sterile sense. Chmielewski also goes to great lengths to consider both comfort and craft in every product, employing details like Japanese denim and Loro Piana cashmere into the brand’s range. So when it comes to tackling an established iconic product, how does Haven do it?

“If you were to think of a farm-to-table kind of approach, it's like using the best ingredients to make the best food. And we're always thinking about that approach as well from a product standpoint,” Chmielewski says. The sneakers are all about subtle details that sum up to a better experience of something that was already pretty great to begin with. A tonal color palette combines different textures of leather, cashmere suede and hairy suede, giving each pair tactile depth that only becomes more pronounced with wear. The Chuck Taylor’s signature rubber toe cap is also replaced with a natural white leather toe cap, a detail that would go undetected more than five feet away. Practically, Haven’s also added an easy-access side-zip made from high-quality custom YKK Excella zippers as well as an additional rubber sole for longevity.

The full magnitude of the sneaker’s design is left for the wearer to experience. Details like reinforced vamps and eyestays, soft leather lining, and an upgraded Ortholite cushioned insole make the shoes more than just pretty to look at.

”The crew at Haven are just so good at translating their signature aesthetic across all products they touch,” says Matt Sleep, Design Lead for Converse Energy. “You see the shoes and instantly you know it fits into their aesthetic ecosystem. You just know it’s Haven without needing to see a logo wildly emblazoned anywhere.”

For a modern label rooted in the classics, the Chuck Taylor is a fitting project. Because, for Chmielewski, it’s all about making things that will last a long time. From the components to the iconic silhouette, you can bet you’ll see a pair of these knocking around for years to come.

#6594. Get to Know the Watchmaker Behind John Mayer’s Latest Pick-Up

When looking for the next big thing in the watch world, there are few better places to check than John Mayer’s wrist. The super collector can make his own Audemars Piguet Royal Oaks, skyrocket the value of a previously underappreciated Rolex Daytona, and help establish new indies. This week, Mayer is co-signing a hyper-limited-edition piece from FVF Genève, a watchmaker you should get to know.

FVF Genève is the brainchild of Spanish-born, Geneva-based watchmaker Franc Vila. Mayer is wearing his latest release: FVF2 Time & Day “Happy Monday,” made in partnership with American watch and jewelry retailer Material Good. On his Instagram, Mayer referred to the collaborators as a “Trifecta of Greatness.” There’s more to this piece than its mesmerizing mother-of-pearl, though. The watch’s design celebrates the idea that, if you love what you do, Monday mornings are actually something to look forward to.

The “Happy Monday” is a limited edition of seven pieces, each of which is engraved with a different day of the week on its rotor. The design is a reminder, as the brand says, that “each day is an opportunity to embrace our calling.” It helps, of course, that this message is delivered by a truly beautiful movement with black-polished surfaces, plenty of beveling and polishing, and great typography. Then there’s the rad day-of-the-week indicator on the dial. Situated between 6 and 9 o’clock, it takes the shape of a subtle gold track with a letter for each day of the week in French. To go with the “Happy Monday” theme, “Lundi” (Monday in French) is the only day represented by a standout green letter.

The dial is the showstopping element on this piece. It’s executed in a sparkly deep-blue mother-of-pearl and accented with thick gold-tone printing in the form of an outer minute track, a sub-seconds display between 4 and 5 o’clock, and bisecting lines that create a classically inspired “sector” design. The interplay of the sector when combined with mother-of-pearl is unusual enough, but add in the retrograde day-of-the-week indicator, and you’ve got a truly compelling combo.

The watch’s 39.5mm case is made out of Grade 5 titanium and features a Titalyt treatment—an electrochemical surface treatment that creates a ceramic-like layer and increases durability and hardness. F.P. Journe is a big fan of this treatment, and FVF uses it to great effect here. The finishing gives the Happy Monday a dark, industrial aesthetic that plays off the mother-of-pearl and gold tones on the dial for a distinctive feel. The watch comes on a matching beads-of-rice bracelet with straight endlinks, further adding to the interplay between vintage and modern inspiration. Finally, the crown and date corrector are located on the left side of the case rather than the right, where they typically sit.

Limited to just seven pieces—not including a unique piece that went to Material Good’s Yoni Ben-Yehuda—the $125,000 Happy Monday is the latest independent watch to receive a co-sign from super-collector John Mayer. Despite his role as Audemars Piguet's “Creative Conduit," Mayer has been known to support high-end independent makers such as F.P. Journe, and famously helped propel Vanguart onto the horological stage over the past year.

Vila, who established his eponymous luxury watch brand in the early 2000s, is a prime candidate to receive his flowers from the modern collecting community: marrying avant-garde case and dial designs with high complications. Vila sold his initial brand in the late 2000s, but he’s now having another go at creating modern classics with FVF. He’s come at the right time. It’s boom times for independent watchmakers as collectors try to identify the next big thing, and a co-sign from Mayer makes FVF a strong candidate to catch fire.

#6593. The Secret to Kendall Jenner’s ‘Me Mode’

The model and founder shares her favorite ways to unwind and how the Therabody TheraFace Mask Glo fits into her nightly routine.

For Kendall Jenner, “Me Mode” is a time to unplug from the daily demands of work and social obligations and simply be still. “I have a really busy mind, so switching off has never come naturally to me,” says the model and entrepreneur. “I’ve had to build little rituals that help me slow down.”

One of those rituals involves Therabody’s TheraFace Mask Glo, an LED face mask that bridges skincare with wellness. Delivering full LED coverage across the entire face, including the lips and under eyes, the cordless device features 504 red, infrared, and blue LEDs, plus a relaxing scalp massage to help relieve tension. Best of all, treatment time is only 12 minutes, giving Jenner a quick, easy, and much-needed pause from her busy schedule.

“After a long day, it’s sweatpants, my dogs, and zero plans,” Jenner says. “Putting on the Mask Glo has kind of become my signal that the day is over. For those 12 minutes, my brain finally goes quiet.”

One thing Jenner loves about the TheraFace Mask Glo is how effortlessly it fits into her routine. “It’s hands-free, so I just put it on and do whatever I feel like that night,” Jenner says. “Sometimes that’s music or journaling, and a lot of the time it’s doing absolutely nothing. The scalp massage is my favorite part. It feels less like a skincare step and more like actually relaxing.”

It offers legitimate skincare benefits, too. Backed by the largest clinical study of any LED mask on the market, the TheraFace Mask Glo was shown to reduce under-eye wrinkles and fine lines, enhance radiance, and lift sagging skin in as little as eight weeks.

The TheraFace Mask Glo offers three LED settings to target different skin concerns. Red light helps improve the appearance of fine lines, wrinkles, and dark spots, while red and infrared light work together to boost collagen production. Blue light targets acne-causing bacteria, helping prevent future breakouts.

The key is consistent use, which Jenner has found easy to maintain. “If a routine is too complicated, I’m not going to stick with it, and I’ve learned that consistency matters more than anything,” she says. “With the Mask Glo, I pick red, red and infrared, or blue light depending on how my skin is acting, and that’s it. It’s easy enough that I actually use it, which is half the battle for me. It comes with me when I travel now, too.”

The LED lights are placed across the entire face, even covering overlooked areas like the mouth and eyes. The preset treatment runs for 12 minutes, cycling through four minutes of each light setting. Four-minute individual treatments are also available.

Combining advanced skincare and relaxation into one simple step, the TheraFace Mask Glo is ideal for anyone who wants to level up their nighttime routine with minimal effort. As Jenner has learned over the years, less is more when it comes to beauty and wellness.

“I’ve been sitting in makeup chairs since I was 14, so I went through a phase of trying everything,” she says. “Now I do a lot less, and I’m more intentional about what I put on my skin. I try to give it a break when I can, and I’ll use the Mask Glo before glam on shoot days.”

Jenner’s nighttime routine is just one aspect in living a more holistic lifestyle. “Wellness for me is mostly about balance now: being at the barn with my horses, getting outside, and protecting my nights,” she says. “My friends make fun of me for going to bed so early, but I’m not changing.”

#6592. The 5 Wellness Trends That Will Define 2027

In 2026, wellness hit new heights. We maxxed protein and creatine and leveled up our supplement stacks. GLP-1s were seemingly everywhere, so was the topic of peptides. As optimization dominated the conversation, a backlash simultaneously grew. Longevity remained a core pursuit, on land and at sea, aided by innovations in tech.

“The tectonic plates in culture are shifting under our feet,” says Lestat McCree, co-founder and CEO of UK-based wellness retailer Healf. “We say that the run club is now becoming the new nightclub, and weekends are full of saunas and ice baths. [Wellness is] the cultural mainstream, and people are really seeing this as the new way to live.”

Young consumers are gravitating towards in-person micro-communities. It’s an opportunity for agencies and brands that get it right.

The global wellness market, now valued at $2.7 trillion, according to McKinsey, shows no sign of slowing down. McKinsey’s Future of Wellness 2027 report, released in November 2026, found wellness is increasingly important across generations, including for consumers previously less engaged. (Forty-nine percent of baby boomers now say wellness is a top priority, up 11 percentage points from 2024, compared with an average five-point increase across other generations.)

Looking ahead, 2027 is poised to be a breakthrough year for many of the nascent shifts that have steadily gained traction in recent years. The 2027 wellness consumer is notably discerning: they’re more informed, more intentional, and more questioning than those who came before. We spoke with analysts, forecasters and industry leaders to unpack the consumer shifts set to define wellness for the year ahead.

In 2027, wellbeing will get personal. Personalization is the defining wellness trend for Healf’s McCree, a thematic shift echoed across almost every report analyzed. This means that instead of stocking up on a slate of generic supplements and products made for a one-size-fits-all approach, wellness regimens will be increasingly informed by an individual’s unique biology, lifestyle, and behavioral preferences.

Tracking and diagnostics are on the rise, but notably, it’s moving beyond wearables. First-time orders of personalized products, like those that track blood, vaginal microbiome and fertility hormones, and at-home test kits for blood, genetics and microbiomes, are all on the rise.

Consumers are tracking key markers with at-home blood testing kits.

McKinsey’s Future of Wellness 2027 report similarly identified diagnostics as a key trend, spanning at-home lab kits, advanced imaging and biomarker panels. Of the 10,000-plus consumers surveyed across China, Germany, the US, and the UK, 34% entered the category this past year, with 51% planning to increase spending.

“[There’s] a shift from tracking to targeted, measurable outcomes,” says Sara Hudson, partner at McKinsey and one of the report’s authors. She expects this approach to move from niche to mainstream next year: consumers will want proof that something works, rather than more data for its own sake.

In 2027, expect wellbeing to be increasingly supported by our environment. With light predicted to be used “as a supplement” in Healf’s What’s Next in Wellbeing: 2027 report, and silence forecast as a luxury trend by strategic foresight consultancy The Future Laboratory, consumers are tipped to use environmental elements as strategic levers for wellbeing.

“[The trend of using] light as a supplement points to how consumers’ understanding of wellbeing is growing ever more holistic,” says Daniel Teweles, head of communications at Healf. “As humans, we evolved in relationship to light, and we’ve largely forgotten that, living largely indoors, particularly in the Northern hemisphere.”

Light products are gaining traction: SAD (seasonal affective disorder) and bright-light therapy lamps, dawn-simulating wake-up lamps and alarm clocks like the TikTok-viral Hatch, and blue light-blocking glasses are all seeing a rise in interest. The growth coincides with rising interest in circadian rhythms, up 72.5% year-on-year, per Spate data.

Silence is also set to take the spotlight. This is anticipated to be visible in an increase in spaces designed for minimal sensory stimulation. “Experiences such as Silent Koli’s guided walks in Finland and the UK’s Sacred Tree darkroom retreat hotel signal an emerging appetite for sensory relief,” says Seyi Oduwole, foresight analyst and author of The Future Laboratory’s Future Forecast 2027 report, set to be released in December. “For 2027, I expect more hotels and wellness spaces to make reducing noise, light and stimulation a core part of their offer.”

Silent Koli offers a low sensory experience with their guided walks in Koli National Park.

Hormone health and male fertility may have been the breakout themes in recent years, but in 2027, they’re set to become mainstream. For women, hormone health has moved beyond fertility and menopause into a core consideration of overall wellbeing.

For Lucy Goff, founder and CEO of MedTech company LYMA, this is a key trend. “In 2027, I expect women’s health to become an increasingly important area of investment [for brands], not simply because it represents a commercial opportunity, but because there is a genuine need for better research, better products and more effective whole system solutions.”

LYMA has branched into offering elastin-stimulating lasers after first developing its health supplements.

Oura is one such example. Following the introduction of new hormonal health features in recent years, including menopause insights and contraceptive tracking, its planned acquisition of AI-native healthcare platform Counsel Health deepens its investment in women’s health. Expected to close by the end of the year, the acquisition is set to further integrate biometric data with physician-led care, with reproductive health identified as a key area of focus.

Demand in hormone health is already visible. Cycle and PMS supplements, inositol supplements, the compound often used to support hormonal conditions like Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS), and perimenopause supplements are shaping the market.

Arrae, a supplement brand targeting gut, hormonal and general women’s health, is now offering hair growth protein.

Male fertility was also predicted by Healf as an emerging trend for 2027, as men increasingly take a more active role in contraception. For many, there’s an increased correlation between fertility and overall wellbeing, with male fertility supplements like Wild Nutrition’s Fertility Support for Men and WeNatal’s For Him supplement seeing sales rise.

If GLP-1s and weight loss medications dominated the wellness conversation in 2026, in 2027, expect to see a second wave. Not necessarily through GLP-1s themselves, but the products used alongside them.

McKinsey forecasts this will grow into an established GLP-1 ecosystem in 2027. “It’s essentially all the products and services that support someone taking GLP-1s. Sometimes these products are specifically designed or developed for GLP-1 users, but often they’re existing products that address the same needs and are increasingly being marketed to GLP-1 users (as well as more broadly).”

While this year saw a boom in the hair loss category and collagen-boosting skincare (with #Collagen amassing 4.8 million views on TikTok), elastin is anticipated to be the next “it” player in skincare. Beyond elastin, Spate forecasts KPV and KLOW peptides to surge in 2027. While these are often associated with GLP-1 use for addressing gut and skin inflammation, tissue repair, and elasticity, Spate suggests this shift points to a broader trend of peptides moving from biohacker forums to the beauty shelf in 2027.

Consumers are also anticipated to increasingly look to what’s next: while general social interest in GLP-1s is down 22.1% from its mid-2025 peak per Spate data, searches for GLP-1 supplements and next-generation compounds like retatrutide are surging, up 265.4% and 501.3% year-on-year, respectively.

Fiber, which supports satiety, is also forecast for growth. Pinterest searches for “high-fiber meals” increased 310% year-on-year, while psyllium husk was named a “breakout ingredient” by Healf. “We see a lot of people using psyllium husk for satiety,” notes Healf’s Teweles. “[This] is likely a response to GLP-1s and how much they’re increasingly dominating the cultural conversation.”

Pinterest searches for “high fiber meals” are on the rise.

For years, wellness has been defined by data and outcomes. But in 2027, the push against quantification — a trend that’s been steadily gaining traction in the past year — may experience its cultural breakthrough. “Wellness brands have spent years selling people more things to do, buy and measure,” says Tom Garland, strategist and founder of brand consultancy Edition+Partners. “The next competitive advantage will be how much they take off your plate.”

For Garland, “subtraction” is the defining word for wellness in 2027. In practice, this looks like wellness offerings that integrate with life, instead of consuming them. “I expect belonging, demonstrable usefulness, and better design around real bodies and life stages to matter more. The opportunity is to help people live well without making wellness their whole life.”

“We’re past peak-optimization,” says Anu Lingala, strategist and author of trend strategy newsletter What’s Anu. “Over the past couple of years, [there’s been] more of an anti-tech attitude culturally in response to AI.” As consumers seek analog options — evident in viral TikTok hashtags like #SlowLiving, #Analogue and #Journalling — presence and experience hold greater weight.

The minimalist Balance phone reflects a growing anti-tech sentiment amongst consumers.

The Future Laboratory also anticipates this shift, as Oduwole explains: “We expect greater emphasis on bodily awareness, pleasure and real-world connection, creating opportunities for wellness experiences that help people feel grounded.”

She points to emerging spaces that prioritize presence and connection as a core way this trend may be expressed. “Photography-free events such as Playbody’s encourage participants to reconnect with how an experience feels… For 2027, I expect presence itself to become a more valuable part of the wellness offer.”

This appetite for presence and pleasure extends to wellness products themselves. Spate predicts grown-up comfort objects as an emerging trend for the year ahead, with interest in weighted stuffed animals up 177.9% year-on-year and weighted eye masks surging over 1,000%, largely driven by TikTok. “Adults are embracing weighted, tactile products as tools for calm,” explains Atkinson. “We see this as part of a broader shift toward sensory wellness, where how a product feels is as important as what it does.”

It’s a sentiment echoed by Healf’s McCree. “2027 will be the year where wellness is less prescribed, less prescriptive and more personal,” he says. “[It’s] less rules and more joy.”

#6591. Birkenstock Clogs Are Easier to Dress Up Than You Think

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Birkenstock clogs have never really gone out of style, but when skinny jeans were replaced with wide-leg and bootcut jeans, they firmly reclaimed their place on the shoe rack. Now that sneakers go way more places than the gym and the grocery store, you should give your Birkenstocks another glance and see your Bostons as a fashion opportunity.

Plus, Birkenstocks have gone far beyond the taupe Boston—the label has made clog variations like the Mary Jane-inspired Maria and modern Loma. Or if you’re still partial to the Boston, you can get the clog style in a variety of cool colors, like Oyster and Thyme, and variations, like big buckles or braided straps.

If you’re not sure how you can transition your Bostons from your throw-on, afterthought shoe, we’re here to help. Below, I’ve compiled some outfit inspiration for you and the pieces you need to re-create it.

Birkenstocks at the office? Absolutely—they are clogs after all, and people wear sneakers to the office all the time. Why wear those flats that give you blisters when your Bostons are right there? Pair them with a coordinating trench and white wide-leg jeans (because we haven’t been following that archaic white-after-Labor-Day rule all fall).

Bernardo Belted Stretch Cotton Trench Coat

Even supermodel and Guest In Residence founder Gigi Hadid can’t resist a comfy pair of Birks. For a perfectly executed, effortless, and casual look, pair your Bostons with a graphic tee and bootcut jeans. Create some visual interest by tying your cardigan or sweatshirt like Hadid, instead of simply around your neck. Now that Bostons are everywhere again, opt for a color like Oyster to set yourself apart from the Taupe pack.

Birkenstocks with a matching sweater set? Hear me out—I’m going to cite stylist Allison Bornstein’s “wrong shoe theory.” It’s been around for a while, but wearing a historically “wrong” shoe with an outfit is often so, so right. You probably have never thought about pairing your Birkenstocks with a skirt, but if you go monochrome, like I’m suggesting, it creates a visually interesting outfit. I suggest opting for Birkenstock’s Maria, a Mary Jane-esque variation on the Boston, if you want a sleeker silhouette.

Everyone has a comfy errands uniform—myself included—but instead of slipping on those track pants or leggings with your Birks for the umpteenth time, maybe elevate your look with some silk pants and a designer suede tote or deviate from the Birkenstock Boston. I recommend checking out the Loma, a new wrap-style clog silhouette from the brand, a modern and playful take on the classic Boston.

Take a page out of this off-duty model’s playbook. Don’t be afraid to mix neutral tones, like cream, black, and gray. The mélange of textures—the suede clogs, colored denim, heather polo, and quilted bag—creates an effortlessly cozy look. Trust me, you’ll be wearing this on repeat on the weekends this fall and winter.

#6590. Rosalía Co-Signs One of This Year’s Most Viral Looks at the Latin Grammys

Rosalía is having a heavenly year, and she has the wardrobe to match. At last night’s Latin Grammy Awards in Las Vegas, the Spanish superstar, who took home a suite of awards including Album of the Year for Lux and Song of the Year for “La Perla,” delivered a series of fantastical, sent-from-above fashion moments.

First up? A gloriously frothy white creation from Matières Fécales, one of the year’s most talked-about—and increasingly celebrity-beloved—fashion labels. Styled by Chloe and Chenelle, Rosalía arrived in a custom gown inspired by the Paris-based label’s spring 2027 collection. The look featured a sheer, tightly ruched corset bodice, clouds of tulle billowing around the shoulders, and an enormous, floor-sweeping skirt. It compounded much of the star’s ongoing aesthetic, which oscillates between bridal confection, prima ballerina, and celestial apparition. Right at home in the spiritually charged universe of Lux.

Matières Fécales, the provocative label founded by Hannah Rose Dalton and Steven Raj Bhaskaran, has quickly become something of a red-carpet phenomenon. Lady Gaga brought its gothic sensibilities to the Grammys earlier this year in a dramatic black feathered gown; Zendaya wore a winged, goddess-like white creation to The Odyssey premiere, and a frayed salmon-pink gown while promoting The Drama. Demi Moore embraced its more extravagant side in a hot-pink Cannes ballgown, while Sarah Paulson and María Zardoya both chose the label for the 2026 Met Gala. There’s a mesmerizing balance of the grotesque and the gorgeous, with shredded fabrics and surreal proportions that coexist with sweeping, exquisitely feminine silhouettes. Rosalía, naturally, is game.

The look fits into the singer’s ever-ambitious fashion vocabulary. Her Lux era has seen her fully embrace the possibilities of fashion as performance, spanning everything from religious iconography to the delicate discipline of ballet. For her tour, Jonathan Anderson created a suite of extraordinary custom Dior costumes, including an embellished organza tutu, a pale-blue pannier dress, a militaristic ensemble with a tricorne hat, and an angel-wing cape. Another heavenly look came courtesy of Argentinian designer Sofía Abadi; Rosalía stepped out wearing her stand-out signature Angel jacket, with its hand-knitted cascade of interlocking and braided cream woolen fringe to create a winged effect. Ballet has also spilled into her off-duty wardrobe: recall the latex-and-tulle tutu dress by emerging designer Yasmina Atta, or her towering archival Junko Shimada ballet platforms.

And what makes Rosalía’s style so exciting is her willingness to champion both the established and the experimental. Alongside the grand maisons, she’s worn emerging names like Monique Fei, Rosalie Bernard, the aforementioned Abadi, and Laura Andraschko, while also indulging in archival McQueen and Nicolas Ghesquière-era Balenciaga. While adventurous, she retains an elegance and ethereality.

The Matières Fécales gown was only the beginning. For her opening performance, Rosalía changed into a custom Erdem gown in a rich, shimmering chartreuse-gold—one of fashion’s most irresistible colors of the moment—with a structured corset, romantic off-the-shoulder bows, and a full, gathered skirt. Later, she returned to the stage to accept her awards wearing ivory Vivienne Westwood Couture: a lace, corseted gown with a delicate high-neck collar and an asymmetric skirt. She closed the evening in a black satin Dior slip dress by Jonathan Anderson, posing and beaming with her awards. Felicidades!

#6588. Ana de Armas’s Complete Dating History

From Ben Affleck to Tom Cruise and beyond.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Ana de Armas has experienced a stratospheric rise in Hollywood over the past decade. 2015’s Knock Knock—a thriller starring Keanu Reeves—provided the Cuban, American, and Spanish actress with her stateside breakout role. Since then, de Armas has appeared in numerous box office and critical hits, such as 2017’s Blade Runner 2049, 2019’s Knives Out, 2021’s No Time to Die, 2022’s Blonde, and 2025’s John Wick spin-off Ballerina.

Offscreen, the actress has had several public romances, too. Most recently, she has been linked to Venezuelan singer Beto Montenegro, with the pair photographed kissing during a summer getaway in Spain. In November 2026, they made their first red carpet appearance together at the Latin Recording Academy’s Person of the Year Gala in Las Vegas.

Here’s what you need to know about Ana de Armas’s dating history.

Prior to making it big as a Hollywood actress, de Armas relocated from Havana to Spain, where she met her first husband, Marc Clotet. The Ghosted star began dating the Spanish model and actor in 2010, with the pair marrying the following year in July 2011, Hola! magazine reported.

Unfortunately, the couple’s marriage didn’t last. During an appearance at the 27th Goya Awards in Spain on Feb. 17, 2013, Clotet revealed, “Yes, we’ve broken up. It was by mutual agreement. I’m calm.” According to Diez Minutos, Clotet also shared that he and de Armas were “still friends” despite the split.

According to La Razón, de Armas started dating Spanish screenwriter and director David Victori in August 2013. The publication also noted that the couple lived together in Los Angeles, but had returned to Spain in March 2014 for the Málaga Film Festival. Although it’s unclear when Victori and de Armas ended their relationship, it’s been reported that they split sometime in 2014.

Following her breakups from Clotet and Victori, de Armas decided to move to Los Angeles full time to further her career, telling The Hollywood Reporter, “I don’t like feeling stuck, like I’m not going anywhere. I wanted more.”

After permanently relocating to America, de Armas began “a serious relationship with agent Franklin Latt,” Vanity Fair reported. During her interview with the publication, the War Dogs actress was quick to dispel the idea that dating a successful Hollywood agent—Latt now manages Pedro Pascal at Creative Artists Agency—aided her career in any way. “For anyone who ever questions...how did I get to do this or that, fuck them,” she said. “They will not get to spend their New Year’s with me. They are not the people whose opinion I should care about. They are not the people I share my happiness with.”

In 2017, de Armas started dating artist Alejandro Piñeiro Bello, who was also born in Havana. During their relationship, the pair regularly posted photos of one another on social media, which have since been deleted from their respective accounts.

In February 2018, de Armas marked the launch of Piñeiro Bello’s pop-up exhibition in Los Angeles by writing on Instagram, “So proud of you,” and he returned the favor, thanking the actress for all of her “hard work and love,” according to Antena 3.

Porter later confirmed that de Armas had split from Piñeiro Bello in 2019 after two years of dating.

After meeting on the set of thriller Deep Water in late 2019, de Armas started a very public relationship with Ben Affleck. In March 2020, a source told People that the pair had “great chemistry right from the start,” but “there were no signs of romance” until filming had wrapped. In a March 2020 interview with Vogue Spain (translated by People), de Armas discussed working with the Oscar winner, saying, “His talent is infinite.” The same month, de Armas made her relationship with Affleck official when she shared photos of him on Instagram.

Affleck and de Armas were regularly photographed walking their dogs together in Los Angeles, where the couple quarantined together during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

In June 2020, de Armas and Affleck attended a Black Lives Matter march together, per People. Following a double date with Affleck’s best friend, Matt Damon, and his wife, People reported that de Armas officially moved into her boyfriend’s property in August 2020. “She’s aware that his family comes first,” a source told the outlet. “And appreciates that. They work very hard at that balance.” For Affleck’s 48th birthday, the Overdrive actress gave her beau a custom-built BMW motorcycle, according to People.

In November 2020, the pair traveled to New Orleans for reshoots of their movie Deep Water. As de Armas appeared to be wearing a diamond ring in photos from the set, rumors started to swirl regarding a possible engagement. However, according to People, the jewelry item was simply a prop for the film. The very same month, de Armas and Affleck spent their first Thanksgiving together, along with the actor’s three children—Violet, Fin, and Samuel—whom he shares with ex-wife Jennifer Garner, E! News reported.

Unfortunately, by January 2021, de Armas and Affleck had called it quits. “Ben is no longer dating Ana,” a source told People. “She broke it off. Their relationship was complicated. Ana doesn’t want to be Los Angeles-based and Ben obviously has to since his kids live in Los Angeles.” People reported that the breakup occurred “over the phone.” Soon after the split, Affleck reconnected with his ex Jennifer Lopez.

Following her split from Affleck, de Armas was romantically linked to Tinder executive Paul Boukadakis in June 2021. In December 2021, an insider told E! News that the couple’s romance was “very serious.”

A July 2022 profile of de Armas in ELLE revealed that she met her new boyfriend “during the pandemic through a mutual friend.” With the majority of bars and restaurants closed during lockdown, they “spent their first dates at each other’s homes, drinking wine and talking.”

As for how she spent her 34th birthday in April 2022, de Armas told ELLE that she celebrated with “my man, my dogs, Chris [Evans] and the crew [of Ghosted].” She continued, “I wasn’t home having a romantic dinner; I was on set with my people doing what I love and at the beach and having a shot of Fireball...and it is the happiest I’ve been.”

The pair was pictured arriving at the Venice Film Festival in September 2022, and they posed for photos on the red carpet at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party on March 12, 2023. While it’s unclear when de Armas and Boukadakis ended their romance, People reported the split in November 2024, when the actress was spotted kissing another man.

The Exposed star surprised fans when she started dating Manuel Anido Cuesta, the stepson of Cuba’s president, Miguel Díaz-Canel Bermúdez. Having graduated with a law degree from the University of Havana in 2019, Anido Cuesta reportedly “became part of the Cuban regime’s inner circle,” La Nación reported. The outlet further explained, “Although he does not hold official positions in government institutions, he has been seen at numerous events and on official trips accompanying his stepfather and mother.”

Rumors began circulating about a potential romance between de Armas and Anido Cuesta in May 2024, when a Cuban influencer claimed the pair had spent 10 days together on the island of Cayo Santa María, off the north coast of Cuba, per Periódico Cubano. While the majority of de Armas’s romance with Anido Cuesta remained private, Hola! published photographs of the pair kissing one another during a night out in Madrid in November 2024. Breakup reports ultimately surfaced in May 2025.

Mission: Impossible icon Tom Cruise and de Armas first sparked dating rumors in winter 2025. The two actors had been spending time together due to work.

While promoting her John Wick spin-off Ballerina in June 2025, de Armas commented on her connection with Cruise, telling Variety, “We’re working together, so he got to see Ballerina and he actually really liked it.” She continued, “It is very special that someone like him is supporting [Ballerina].”

In mid-July 2025, a source downplayed the romance rumors, telling People that de Armas and Cruise simply had “a special work relationship.” According to the insider, the pair had been spending extended periods of time together while preparing to co-star in the thriller Deeper, from the director of 2005’s Mr. & Mrs. Smith, Doug Liman. “Tom is an incredible mentor to Ana,” the source alleged. “She has nothing but amazing things to say about him.”

The end of July brought two eyebrow-raising outings for de Armas and Cruise. On July 26, the pair made an unexpected cameo at an Oasis concert in London, appearing in the background of an Instagram video shared by music producer Goldie. The following day, de Armas and Cruise materialized in Vermont, where they were photographed holding hands, eating ice cream, and shopping together.

In October 2025, People reported that de Armas and Cruise were only ever friends. A source said Cruise was a “dear friend and mentor” to her and added, “She’s single, though, and has been for a while. She stays in touch with Tom and they still have an upcoming movie project that she’s looking forward to.”

De Armas sparked romance rumors with Venezuelan singer Beto Montenegro in summer 2026. The pair was seen together at a concert in Madrid, where Hola! captured a video of them dancing on July 29.

The speculation intensified in August when de Armas and Montenegro traveled to Formentera, Spain. On August 2, they were photographed holding hands and kissing while making their way to the beach.

On November 11, de Armas and Montenegro made their red carpet debut together at the Latin Recording Academy’s 2026 Person of the Year Gala in Las Vegas.

The actress wore a black Wiederhoeft look featuring a corseted top and sheer lace skirt, while Montenegro opted for a black suit with a light blue shirt and dark tie.

#6587. Truman Capote’s Zoo, From a 1976 Issue of Vogue

Editor’s Note: Looking through the archive it feels like Truman Capote was almost as much in Vogue as he was hobnobbing with his society swans. It’s not surprising to learn that the author of Breakfast at Tiffany’s had a taste for the finer things in life. Some of Capote’s possessions will be sold by Cornell Auctions on November 21. A number of the lots appeared in a 1976 Vogue article, written by Leo Lerman, a virtual tour of “Capote’s Zoo.” Printed in black-and-white in the magazine, we are able to share color pictures of these figurines, and a few that didn’t make the edit.—LBP

“Capote’s Zoo,” by Leo Lerman with photographs by Horst P. Horst, was originally published in the July 1976 issue of Vogue.

Truman’s beasts, 24 of them, complete with Trumanisms, comments on his quarries by their see-all, tell-all keeper.... Three years ago, when Horst took this photograph [seen above], Truman Capote was smiling his I-know-a-secret smile. Now he’s still smiling—but it’s his come-little-ghostie-sit-on-my- knee smile—at the brouhaha over the cliff-hanger publication of his novel Answered Prayers (most recent chapter: “Unspoiled Monsters”), a book about the humans in his zoo.

It’s no secret that Truman Capote—Little T. to those who love him, The Tiny Terror to those who hate-love him—is passionate about secrets: his own, other people’s. His books are rife with them, brought to horrendous or hilarious or exquisite flower. The star-y role he plays in Neil Simon’s movie, Murder by Death, explodes with secrets. And in his apartment and three houses (Manhattan, Long Island, California, Switzerland), Truman has accumulated hundreds of objects—a zoo of beasts, many of which conceal secret repositories—little drawers, infinitesimal hollows.

“I’ve just been collecting for thousands of years,” says Little T.—his speaking voice ranges at least three octaves per sentence, from Little Nell to Old Mischief.  “And I bought all of these animals. I’ve collected them—well, all over the world. Why animals? I love animals per se, in real life.” Maggie, the presiding “real” beast, is a sedately rampageous, hideously attractive English bull, referred to by Capote as “my little doggie.” Little T. continues, “And I like objects, ’specially objects  that are—well, I don’t like them just for themselves. Usually I like them to be something else other than what they are. Like that English dog’s head over there with that cap on his head [Truman sometimes wears one very like it]—he’s one of my favorites, and he’s a tobacco jar. My house at the beach’s got just loads of marvelous, curious objects.”

And that’s what Truman Capote’s Zoo is all about: “marvelous, curious objects,” collected seriously for years—the inanimates like the ones on these pages, the animates in his writings from “Miriam” to Other Voices, Other Rooms to In Cold Blood to Answered Prayers—with its gamy-rich, pants-down fill of look-look-now, isn’t that Lady Κ., B.P., Princess R., T.W.? Isn’t that Little T. just loving them all to death for posterity? ... Little T. smiles seraphically, as he contemplates his zoo, peering at a life-sized, carved wooden tree about whose branches winds a terrifying wooden serpent. “That,” he murmurs sweetly, “came off a Zen temple.”

Below, 24 residents of the Manhattan Branch of Truman Capote’s Zoo, complete with Trumanisms about his creatures.

“It’s yellow, blue, and porcelain all over—this English, Victorian, last-laugh cat.”

“This Russian frog changes into a box.” Even frogs work in Russia.

“An English frog toting an inkwell.” Pumping iron? Even frogs are doing it at T.’s.

“It’s a children’s toy, a wooden, green, rocking parrot that Quakers carved long, long ago.”

“This Japanese ceramic cat is, I believe, seventeenth century.” A seraphic smiler.

“A perfect giraffe—silver, Portuguese....” He’s not a box—just an elegant observer.

“Two Meissen fowls fornicating.” That’s Capote telling it as it is in his zoo.

“I use these Chinese bronze rats as candle holders.” On his dining table, they’re right.

“And this is a Meissen rabbit—German, of course.” A haughty, businesslike bunny.

“What’s blue, white, porcelain all over? This Japanese, eighteenth-century creepy cat.”

“This owl is silver, Italian, eighteenth century....” And won’t talk—even for a mouse.

“This is a Japanese gold chipmunk.” Chipmunks must be different in Japan. Note ears.

“This green thing is Chinese porcelain. And its head moves!” Could be cat, pug?

“A white, horned English porcelain owl. The top opens up—the owl’s a tobacco jar.”

“This Eskimo-carved walrus is actually a box—its interior carved from walrus tusk.”

“One of my favorites, an English tobacco box.” Doggie’s sporting Truman’s hat.

“Japanese fishermen used these to ward off evil spirits.” Answered Prayers can try.

“Hand-carved, ivory Chinese boxes. Fat birds. And they open up!” T. loves that.

“Such a favorite, this Japanese rabbit baying at the moon.” Baying? Only for Little T.

“A tiny, Meissen parrot’s-head box. You open the head....” To find a Tiny Terror secret?

#6586. All About Phoebe Dynevor’s Husband, Cameron Fuller

Phoebe Dynevor became a fan favorite during the first season of Bridgerton. The Netflix show focused on the love story between her character Daphne and Regé-Jean Page’s Simon. Their romance ended with a happily-ever-after, and Dynevor has continued to build her career in Hollywood. Off camera, her romantic life has been flourishing as well. In September 2026, the actress married Cameron Fuller, an actor himself and someone very familiar with the entertainment industry as the son of a famous producer.

Here’s everything to know about Dynevor’s relationship with Fuller so far.

Fuller is the son of producer Brad Fuller, who specializes in horror films like The Purge franchise, A Quiet Place, and A Nightmare on Elm Street. The younger Fuller studied performing in college, receiving a bachelor of arts in theater from the University of Southern California in 2017. He has since appeared on shows like Insecure, Into the Dark, The Goldbergs, and The Last Ship.

In March 2023, Dynevor and Fuller were seen leaving a hotel in New York City together. A month later, they were photographed holding hands in London, eventually meeting up with Fuller’s father for some shopping. A few pics showed some PDA where Fuller’s arms were wrapped around the actress.

In July, they were photographed enjoying Wimbledon.

E! broke the news of their engagement on May 7, 2024, confirming that Dynevor unveiled her engagement ring at the 2024 Met Gala.

In 2022, Fuller was romantically linked to Pretty Little Liars’ Lucy Hale briefly. He also dated influencer Lauren Elizabeth for a few years. In 2021, Dynevor dated Saturday Night Live alum Pete Davidson for five months.

Yes. Dynevor and Fuller left the Corinthia Hotel together and headed to the BAFTAs on Feb. 18, 2024.

Dynevor wore a black top paired with a matching skirt, while Fuller also opted for an all-black look.

Yes. Dynevor confirmed her marriage to Fuller on Sept. 17, 2026, nearly two weeks after the couple reportedly wed in Provence, France, on Sept. 5, 2026. #6585. Ariana Grande and Ricky Alvarez’s Full Relationship Timeline

Nearly a decade after ending their relationship, Ariana Grande and Ricky Alvarez are back in the public eye.

The former couple recently sparked reconciliation rumors after they were spotted spending time together in Texas and Florida during Grande’s Eternal Sunshine Tour. Grande also made multiple changes to the Ricky lyric in “Thank U, Next,” prompting fans to wonder whether the pair had rekindled their romance.

On July 14, People confirmed that they were back on—but taking things slowly. “Ariana has always considered Ricky a friend,” a source told People. “She’s not held ill will against him [since their split]. Ricky is dependable, trustworthy and very supportive. Ariana feels she can be herself around Ricky.”

Grande and Alvarez first met when he joined her as a backup dancer on her 2015 Honeymoon Tour. They dated for about a year before separating in 2016, but have maintained a friendly relationship ever since.

Below, a full timeline of everything we know about Ariana Grande and Ricky Alvarez’s relationship.

Grande and Alvarez met while he worked as a backup dancer on her Honeymoon Tour. They began dating that year.

Grande briefly spoke about their relationship in a Billboard cover story.

“We’re happy,” she said. “I’m a very happy girl. I have a healthy life right now, and I think that’s all anyone cares to know. The end.”

The story also included comments from Grande’s friend Victoria Monét, who shared that “Moonlight” was inspired by the beginning of Grande and Alvarez’s relationship.

“That’s what Ricky called her one night,” Monét said. “I think it was after their first kiss. He waited to kiss her for a long time, and she was really impressed. He’s such a gentleman, and the song is a great little bookmark of the start of their relationship.”

Multiple outlets reported that Grande and Alvarez had ended their relationship after about a year together.

Grande referenced Alvarez in her hit single “Thank U, Next,” singing, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / Now I listen and laugh.”

After the song’s release, Alvarez shared videos of himself reacting to the lyric on Instagram Stories.

“Nothing but gratitude,” he wrote. “Thank you, next… (those songs are fire tho… you’re welcome).”

Grande reposted his Stories and joked about the lyric herself.

“HAHAHAHAHHAHAHAH IM SORRY U GOT THE WORST LINE. It was meant v lovingly.”

When fans later speculated that the pair had reunited after they interacted on Instagram, Grande shut down the rumors herself in the comments of one of Alvarez’s posts.

“We’re friends, everyone take a big ol breather,” she wrote.

Years later, Grande and Alvarez were photographed together in Austin, Texas, ahead of one of her Eternal Sunshine Tour stops. Photos circulating online showed them dining with a group while Grande celebrated her birthday in the city.

According to TMZ, sources familiar with the situation said Alvarez was one of several friends spending time with Grande and that the outing was purely platonic. People also reported that the pair had “been hanging out recently.”

During her Austin concerts, Grande also made noticeable changes to the Ricky lyric in “Thank U, Next.”

Earlier in the week, she sang, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / And they still kinda slap.” At another performance, she changed the line again, singing, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / I know he’s still got my back.”

Over Fourth of July weekend, Grande and Alvarez were photographed shopping together at a Whole Foods in Boca Raton, Florida, before heading to celebrate the holiday with Grande’s family, according to TMZ.

The outing came after Grande wrapped three sold-out Eternal Sunshine Tour shows in nearby Sunrise.

The following day, People published additional details about their friendship, citing a source who said Alvarez has been joining Grande for portions of her tour.

“She’s having a great time on tour. She loves having close friends join her for parts of the tour,” the source said. “Ricky has always been a friend and confidant. She really trusts him. He has such great, positive energy, makes her laugh, and she enjoys spending time with him.”

The source also addressed Grande’s life following her breakup from Ethan Slater.

“Her relationship with Ethan is 100 percent over. She’s focused on her tour and spending time with the people who have always been there for her,” the source said. “Ariana is having the best time reconnecting with fans and loves being onstage.”

Grande fueled reconciliation rumors herself a week later on July 13. She changed the Ricky lyric of “Thank U, Next” again during her Brooklyn show, singing, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / We always find our way back.”

Hours later on July 14, sources confirmed to People and TMZ that they were officially dating again. The insiders told both outlets that they were taking things very slowly.

“They’re not jumping into anything serious right away, but Ari is happy to have him back in her life,” a source told People. The insider added that they “have a similar, smart, dry sense of humor.”

On July 16, Grande and Alvarez were photographed walking in Central Park with their arms wrapped around each other. It marked their first public sighting since news of their reconciliation broke.

On July 17, TMZ shared more pictures of the couple enjoying some PDA from the same day. In the images, Alvarez is embracing Grande as she leans toward him on the street.

Alvarez went out and supported Grande while she performed in Brooklyn. The dancer was spotted at her July 18 and 19 Eternal Sunshine Tour shows. On the second night, he and Grande’s brother, Frankie Grande, had a sweet moment.

On July 27, Grande soft-launched her relationship with Alvarez on Instagram. The singer tagged him in a Polaroid of herself, seemingly giving him credit for taking it.

On August 12, Grande went Instagram official with Alvarez, sharing two photos of them together in a carousel post. “🌱 ！ ♡,” she captioned it.

Days after Grande made her relationship with Alvarez Instagram official, fans noticed that the couple appears to share a meaningful tattoo. During the London stop of her Eternal Sunshine Tour, Grande displayed a new piece across her upper chest reading, “I do love you.” Alvarez has the same phrase tattooed near his collarbone, though his version appears in a different typeface.

A few days later, they were seen in London, where Grande was set to start her 10-day residency. The couple was wearing two cozy layered looks in the cooler U.K. temperatures, with Grande wearing an oversize white cardigan and Alvarez in a jean jacket. They walked arm-in-arm down the street, immersed in conversation.

Grande and Alvarez were also photographed out in London with Grande’s mom, Joan, on August 27. In the photos, Grande and Alvarez walked hand-in-hand as they made their way through the city.

Grande wore a fitted white graphic T-shirt with dark-wash jeans, oversize sunglasses, and a white headband, while Alvarez kept things casual in a white T-shirt, jeans, and a baseball cap. Joan joined them in an all-black look with pink earrings.

During the final show of her Eternal Sunshine Tour at London’s O2 Arena, Grande gave Alvarez another shout-out while performing “Thank U, Next.”

When she reached the lyric about her boyfriend, she changed the original line to, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / I’m tryna make him my last.”

That same week, Alvarez shared his photos from Grande’s tour, including one of her kissing his hand in what appears to be a dressing room. He otherwise captured her in motion, performing onstage.

“It’s the best thing to do,” he wrote in the caption.

The post comes shortly after Grande shared a snippet of them kissing at her rehearsals in London. The intimate moment was part of a video montage she shared at the end of her Eternal Sunshine Tour to thank everyone for what she calls “one of the most beautiful, extraordinary experiences” of her life.

On November 7, Grande shared an Instagram Reel with Alvarez as the couple played a kissing challenge game for her makeup brand, R.E.M. Beauty.

In the video, Grande sat on Alvarez’s lap while he wore a beanie over his eyes and attempted to guess what lip product she was wearing when she kissed him.

“This is a challenge called ‘What’s on my lips?’” Grande explained.

Black Doves is back, and it’s just as action-packed as ever. Netflix’s deadly, dark, and irreverently funny spy thriller follows a covert intelligence organization as it uncovers and sells secrets among the rich and powerful. Season 1 brought us Keira Knightley as the fearless agent Helen; Sarah Lancashire as her icy spymaster, Reed; and Ben Whishaw as an assassin and Helen’s longtime friend.

That first season closed with many loose ends, so it wasn’t a huge surprise when it was announced that we’d be seeing Helen and Sam in action again. This time around, Sam appears as a washed-up hit man taking low-paid jobs, while Helen is still working for the Black Doves—something that proves to be complicated given her husband, Wallace (played by Andrew Buchan), is now prime minister.

All episodes of the new season dropped on Netflix on November 5. If you’re eager to get to know the cast and characters more closely—and are wondering where you might have seen those new faces before—then read on.

As an agent of the Black Doves, Helen Webb is tasked with gathering highly sensitive information obtained via her politician husband, Wallace. But keeping up the image of a good spouse, mother, and spy all at once becomes increasingly difficult to maintain, and Helen grows conflicted about her life of betrayal. You’ll know Keira Knightley, of course, from her career of starry roles in everything from Disney’s Pirates of the Caribbean to Pride & Prejudice, Bend It Like Beckham, and Love Actually.

Helen’s close friend, a previously high-flying hit man, an ex-employee of the Black Doves, Sam Young attempted to leave behind his former life—but that was easier said than done. Now he’s taking low-paid jobs and drinking alone in bars, before he finds himself roped into business with Helen once again. You’ll know Whishaw from his role in Daniel Craig’s James Bond films—Skyfall, Spectre, and No Time to Die—as well as A Very English Scandal and The Hour.

Relentless and cold, the spymaster Reed is Helen’s handler at the Black Doves and does not mess around. In season 2, we see new, more vulnerable sides of her character unfold via glimpses of her younger self and flashes to the past events that came to define her. You’ll recognize Lancashire from her role in Happy Valley.

Wallace Webb is Helen’s husband and the father of her two children, and he’s completely unaware of her career as a Black Dove. In season 2, his own career has taken off and he becomes the U.K.’s prime minister—a move that comes with highly strict security measures in the backdrop of rising tensions in his marriage. Buchan has also starred in Industry, The Crown, and Carnival Row.

Another assassin, Williams, worked for the crime leader Lenny in the first season of Black Doves. This time around, she’s moved on and formed a partnership with Eleanor, following the death of her previous partner, as well as a friendship with Sam. Hyland has starred in Towards Zero, A Thousand Blows, and Tall Tales and Murder.

As Williams’s partner, Eleanor is another fast-footed assassin with a refreshing sense of humor. Creevy has also starred in Amadeus, The Guest, and Operation Mincemeat.

Laila is an assassin with a fun, nonchalant, and lighthearted personality—a contrast to Helen, whom she clashes with at the start of season 2. You’ll know Ambika Mod for her roles in This Is Going to Hurt and as the co-lead of Netflix’s One Day adaptation.

Mr. Conteh is a senior at Black Doves and is hungry for power. As the fabric of the institution is put under pressure and he is sent to investigate Reed, Conteh becomes increasingly prominent for Helen and her associates. Ceesay has also starred in Alien: Earth.

Cruelly minded and understated in tone, Patrick works for a rival organization to Black Doves, the same group that presents an appealing get-out for Sam when he needs it the most. Riley also starred in the comedy-horror Pride and Prejudice and Zombies as well as Firebrand.

Hard-headed with tunnel vision, Cecile Mason is a U.S. defense envoy, arriving at 10 Downing Street to work on relations between the president and the prime minister ahead of a major peace summit. Campbell was a star of the Scream movies, as well as Party of Five and Wild Things.

Glamorous and sharp-minded, Katia Chernov is the wife of Russian oligarch Alexi Chernov and becomes swept up in the mysteries in the new series. She’s played by Sylvia Hoeks, who has also starred in Blade Runner 2049 and The Girl in the Spider’s Web.

A well-connected Russian oligarch with immeasurable influence and power, Alexi Chernov is a force to be reckoned with in season 2, with fingers in some of the most fragile cases. He’s played by Goran Kostić, whom you may recognize from Ant-Man and the Wasp or Canary Black.

#6583. Before Anything Else, Geoffrey Holder Was a Painter. A New Show Spotlights His Tremendous Body of Work

Geoffrey Holder refused to choose a lane. Born in Trinidad and Tobago in 1930, he was a principal dancer with the Metropolitan Opera Ballet, the first Black man to win Tony Awards for both directing and costume design (for the Broadway hit The Wiz), and the voice and face of 7Up throughout the 1970s and ’80s, all while building a celebrated film career with roles in Doctor Dolittle, Annie, and the Bond film Live and Let Die.

And yet, before everything else, Holder was a painter. “Painting always came first,” says his son, Leo Holder, who oversees the artist’s estate. “Practically everything else he did has always been an extension of this. He was always working on something. At any given time, wherever he was living, there were several canvases in progress.” Still, across his decades-long career, it was the facet of his work that received the least attention.

“Geoffrey Holder: Black Magic,” on view at the Museum of Contemporary Art North Miami from November 18, 2026, to April 4, 2027, aims to correct this. Guest curated by Dr. Erica Moiah James, principal investigator and publication editor for the Geoffrey Holder Project, it’s the first museum survey to center Holder’s work as a visual artist. Bringing together more than 60 works across eight decades, the show offers an unprecedented look at the practice that anchored his entire multidisciplinary career.

Geoffrey Holder, Untitled, n.d. Oil, oil marker, and China marker on wood. 84 x 36 inches.

Influenced by his older brother, Boscoe Holder—himself a painter, designer, dancer, and musician—Geoffrey took up painting in childhood and had his first formal exhibition in Trinidad by the age of 14. According to his son, Holder funded his move to the United States in the early 1950s by selling 20 of his paintings, and when he died in 2014, he left behind more than 250 paintings and 300 collages, along with a trove of drawings, sculptures, and photographs.

The exhibition is the result of more than a decade of work, beginning when James was first invited by Holder’s family to see his archive in 2015. “I knew Geoffrey the way most people knew him,” James tells Vogue. “I had seen his films. I knew he was involved with The Wiz, I had seen the 7Up commercials. But I didn’t know him. What I realized the moment I stepped into his archive is that he knew himself. He understood there would be a moment when people would get it. He might not be there, but he was going to select and preserve the record of his life so that we could really dive into it.”

Geoffrey Holder, Waiting for the Dance, 2001. Oil, pastel crayon, and China marker on Masonite. 48 x 48 inches unframed. 50 ½ x 50 ½ inches framed.

The show takes its title from Holder’s deep interest in what he dubbed “magical people,” those whose creative spirit and sheer presence carried an unmistakable energy. “There’s a negative way of framing Black people as ‘magical Negroes,’ but he wasn’t thinking that way,” James explains. “He thought of it in incredibly positive terms, and was referencing a je ne sais quoi—something almost beyond language, a sort of confidence and way of being in the world that is truly remarkable. So we took the word ‘magic’ and racialized it, because most of the subjects in the exhibition are Black people.”

Occupying the full museum, the show is organized into five sections—Portraits, Epistles, The Sacred and the Profane, Genre, and Figure Studies—pairing the artworks with a rich collection of costume sketches, performance footage, correspondence, and memorabilia that provide historical context while illustrating the breadth and depth of Holder’s creative life.

One standout is Portrait of Carmen (1980), an oil on canvas depicting a stylized Black woman in a sleek black dress and turquoise earrings against a crimson background. The painting reflects not only Holder’s interest in the female figure but also his profound devotion to his wife, the American dancer, choreographer, and actress Carmen de Lavallade, to whom he was married for 59 years, until his death. Also on view is the portrait Woman in Yellow (1985), part of a motif that, according to James, traces back to the first time Holder saw de Lavallade, wearing a yellow dress. “He painted women in various stages of a yellow dress forever,” she says.

Geoffrey Holder and Carmen de Lavallade in 1955, the year they married.

Also central to the show is a series of works that reinterpret biblical stories through Holder’s distinctive lens. Adam and Eve (ca. 1990s), for instance, is a towering diptych in oil, oil marker, and china marker on canvas, in which black tree trunks rise through a dense forest of green leaves; in the lower left corner, two nude figures are nearly swallowed by the foliage. In another large oil painting, Adam and Eve (2000–2005), Holder returns to the same subject, this time creating a more intimate image that foregrounds the couple while still enveloping them in greenery. Holder’s son explains that the artist’s interest in biblical narratives was not, strictly speaking, religious. Instead, “he saw them as a wonderful source of storytelling, theater, and drama.”

Geoffrey Holder, Adam and Eve, 2000-2005. Oil on board. 71 7/8 x 30 inches unframed. 73 ½ x 31 ¼ inches framed.

In another biblically inspired work, John the Baptist and Jesus (undated), Holder depicts the two figures as Black men standing together in cerulean water, sharing a tender moment as a crowd looks on. “This is one of my favorites, because it shows a level of intimacy between Black men—a level of care, gentleness, and tenderness that you just don’t [usually] see out in the world,” James says. “Geoffrey is making a point. He’s appropriating the religious story, but there’s something very contemporary, maybe even a longing for that kind of open expression of care among Black men in the world.”

Reflecting on the interest in his father’s visual art practice more than a decade after his death, Leo Holder says he’s more convinced than ever that, as a multihyphenate, his father was ahead of his time, rarely seen as a serious painter because of his many other creative pursuits. “Nowadays, we have far more of an ecosystem that allows you to be polymathic. And he’s gotten the kind of attention for his art that he never got when he was alive,” he says. “In part, it’s because now everybody’s caught up.”

#6582. These Cozy Shoes Are Too Chic to Keep Indoors

Slippers in public? These fashionable pairs make a convincing case.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

At this point, we’ve all probably accepted that slippers are no longer strictly house shoes. They’ve been part of our everyday wardrobes for years, and it’s hardly unusual to see someone wearing a fuzzy pair of slip-ons with jeans and a nice coat. What’s more interesting is how far brands have taken the idea lately. And honestly, some of these new styles are just really good shoes, slippers or not.

Take Ugg’s Western-inspired designs. Cowboy boots aren’t going anywhere, and the brand has found a way to bring that look into the comfortable footwear it’s known for. It’s a fun alternative to a traditional Western boot, especially if you want something a little more relaxed for everyday wear.

Brunch’s collaboration with Madhappy is another one worth knowing about. The two brands share co-founder Joshua Sitt, so the partnership makes sense, but the shoes themselves are what caught our attention. Made with colorful crochet and lined with shearling, they look like someone turned a chunky knit sweater into a slipper. And considering how much we love a good sweater this time of year, why shouldn’t our feet get a sweater of their own?

For Sitt, the idea of making slippers part of an everyday wardrobe has always been central to Brunch. “Originally, the entire concept for the brand was taking the hotel slipper product which is famously associated with vacation and travel, and bringing it into something you can wear every single day inside and outside of your home,” he tells ELLE.

You can see that thinking at work in the Madhappy collaboration. “The shoe itself morphs the comfort that both brands prioritize as well as the fashion pieces of both brands,” he says.

What’s particularly interesting is that this isn’t limited to brands you’d normally associate with slippers. Hunter, whose rain boots have been a wardrobe staple for years, has a cozy option of its own. Simkhai has entered the category, too, and Alo has a pair that feels especially fitting for the Pilates-to-coffee crowd. It’s a pretty good indication of just how much room there is to play with a shoe that used to be purely practical.

The styling is arguably the best part. A Western-inspired pair would look great with straight-leg jeans and a suede jacket, while a softer, more understated slipper can make tailored trousers and a wool coat feel less formal. You don’t need to rethink your wardrobe to wear them. In fact, that’s part of the appeal.

As Sitt points out, slippers haven’t exactly been the most considered purchase in our wardrobes. Ask people what pair they own, and “you’ll get some crickets,” he says. Or maybe they “stole a pair at a wedding.” No offense to wedding favors, but we think it’s time for an upgrade.

Whether you’re looking for an alternative to your usual boots or simply want a pair of slippers you won’t want to change out of before leaving the house, these are the styles worth a closer look. Shop our favorites below.
